They are content to let the menfolk of their neighbours do all the fighting and the Suffering. The outrages committed by. the Germans in France and Belgium are terrible, but they argue that somehow or other we shall prevent such horrors and devastation reaching our own hearts and homes, without the help of those they love. The fear of their risking life or limb is, perhaps, natural, and there are ex- ceptions to every general rele, hut no woman with patriotic instincts should stand in the way of her male friends or relatives, who desire to _enlist, even if she cannot bring herself to urge them to go.

div.head: WORKINGMEN'S MISSION.
div.p: WORKINGMEN'S MISSION.
Visit of Mrs. John Crosfield.
BELGIUM THE MODERN SPARTA.

The annual meeting and social gathering of the Working Men's Mission, Bank Quay, took place on Monday evening at the Mission Rooms. The proceedings, besides being of a very happy nature and 'marked by the presence of several members of the,Crosfield family, who irtve done so much for the Institute, were memorable on account of the attendance of several Belgian refugees, who are the honoured guests of the Mission. These representatives of our heroic Allies appeared to thoroughly enjoy the pro- gramme, and especially' Mrs. John Crosfield's graciousness in speaking to them in their own language..

There were about 200 people present, includ- ing Mrs. john Crosfield (who presided), Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Crosfield (who paid a welcome sur- prise visit), Mr. C. E. Parker, Mr. G. Dale, Mr. T. Dale, and Mr. A. Tilling (secretary)..

Mr. George Dale, who presided • pro tern., pending .the arrival of Mrs. John, Crosfield (Colwyn Bay); said he did not intend to make a speech, and as they - had their ,good friend, Mr. Parker, with them,, had another meet- _ __
_ jag to attend, he would call upon that gentle- man to address them. (Applause.)
BELGIUM LIKENED UNTO SPARTA.

Mr. Parker, who was warmly received, said he would first of all tell them a story which happened two thousand years ago. It was before the Roman Empire came into being. An- other great Empire then almost ruled the world, that was the Empire of Persia. It had spread its conquests almost all over Europe, and there was Only one little country that had not been conquered by the Persians. That was the country of Greece. It was divided into a num- ber of small republics, and at the same time Xerxes; was the great War Lord of Persia- He determined to subjugate by the power of his might the free republics of Greece. For years he prepared , a great army and fleet, and when he had done so he started from Asia to bring about the conquest of Greece. He came to the Dardanelles,' a narrow Stream dividing the Black Sea from the Mediterranean, called at that time the Hellespont. 'Great bridges were built across it to allow his army to cross. Xerxes, when he came to it and saw his great hosts and fleet of, ships about 700—not like our Dreadnoughts, but small fighting boats befitting the time—offered a prayer to God and thanked the Lord for mak- ing him such a great War Lord and prayed for victory. Mrs. Crosfield, who entered at this juncture, was accorded a most- enthusiastic reception.

Mr. Parker, proceeding, expressed the plea- sure of all present at seeing Mrs. Crosfield amongst them. Continuing his story, he said this great army took seven days and seven nights to cross over the Hellespont. Xerxes decided to number his hosts. To do this he massed 10,000 men in close formation, marked a line round them, dismissed these and brought others into the enclosure, and so till the number of the army was found to be 2,500,000. They cattle to the northern boundary of Greece, which was hilly, and had to go through the defile of Thermopyla3 Pass, a great landmark in the history of the world. Greece had here 700 men, against two and a half mil- lion. Xerxes told some of his 'picked, warriors to go and take the 700 Spartans and bring them to him. He despised such a small band being able to stop his army. The picked war- riors went forth, but instead of taking the Spartans they were defeated. Next day he sent his Immortals, or, as we would call them, Life Guards, who had never been " defeated. They also were thrown hack, and this hap- pened day after day. Numbers and treachery told in the end, and the Spartans were reduced to. 300. The ' King Leonidas was killed. The Spartans formed a ring round his body and fought on a little hill against the hosts until every man of them was killed. The heroism. Manifested by the Spartans created such a spirit in the republics of Greece, that, although inferior to Xerxes'..Persitin forces, they were able, aided by the weather, to retain their independence.

div.head: Comparison.
div.p: The Comparison.

During 'the last few months Belgium had fur- nished a striking parallel to the historic achievement of Sparta; They might conceive a parallel between Xerxes and the Emperor William, and draw a comparison between Leonidas, leader of the Spartans, and 'Albert, ging of the Belgians, and his brave General, Leman, the defender of Liege. That narrow pass of • Thermopylm was in many respects similar to that narrow pass through which the "German: Army . had to get into France, i.e., Liege. Just .as •Thermopylre ' had always stood in the history of the world as the point to which all small nations fighting for their freedom have looked back as a landmark for :courage, and have found inspiration, so he thought they and future generations would all look back to the defence which the Belgian people made at Liege. There was little doubt that if it had not been for Belgium holding back the hosts of Germany for eleven days Paris would have been, taken, France over-run and very likely our own country' would have been invaded. He spoke' of these things because of the connection that Church had formed with the Belgian people by preparing a home for a family. He was ;very glad that they had got these people amongst them, and was sure that the associa- tion would be a happy one. They were doing a good work, and every Church in the town ought to be doing the same. (Hear, hear.) It was not a question of: charity or anything of that sort. It was rather a question of receiving as honoured guests people who had, through misfortune, and no fault of their own, been rendered homeless. He had received a letter from a Sergeant-Major in the Belgian Army, whose wife and family they had got amongst their guests. In it the soldier thanked him (the speaker)—although he had nothing to do with it except to form one of the links that .brought the family there—for the kindness extended to his family. This Belgian said lie was proud to fraternise with the English soldiers, and was confident that with their help the Germans would be driven out of Belgium. He ended by saying that the English people had hearts_ of gold; "and I. hope," concluded Mr. Parker, "that you will prove yourselves worthy of that high compliment." (Applause.)

div.head: PROGRESS IN SPITE OF THE WAR. – An Encouraging Report.
div.p: PROGRESS IN SPITE OF THE WAR. - An Encouraging Report.

The Secretary read the annual report, which stated The sorrow of the heart and the turmoil and clash of arms have made us turn more readily to the tranquility and calm of God's House, and His people have been comforted and blessed by the Divine Presence. We have to report that the services throughout the year have been very well attended, and we may truthfully (yet not boastfully) say that, spirit- ually and numerically, the Church was 'never in a better position than at .present. .Our Church' membership increased during the year from 142 to 158, and the average attendance of communicants at the monthly communion ser- vices was 88.

Our position financially is as follows: Balance from 1913, £l7 85.;., income: during 1914,- 4:120 145.; expenditure during 1914, .e.lll 14s. 11d.; balance in hand, .06 is. id. During the last month or so we have, however, incurred an expenditure of ...e4O in the purchase and fixing of an electric organ-blowing apparatus, and the balance will be more than swallowed up in meeting this excrenditure. • Our Mission Extension Fund stands with a credit balance at the bank of .063 9s. 2d.
The Helping Hand:
The Poor Fund is still -Under the supervision of Mr. Thomas Dale, and the funds distributed quietly anti unostentatiously through this source have been much appreciated by the .needy receivers.

The League of help has also distributed over A:l2 in -cash, and also considerable quantities of clothing... It is extremely gratifying to know that the need for assistance in this district is less this winter than it has been for some years, and there appears to .be no lack of work in the town.

' The country's need has 'called many men to arms, and 24 of our young men have enlisted. In the letters we receive from -time to time, grateful references are very often made to the helpful influence of the training and teaching received at the Mission, which is helping them in their new and trying circumstances. Our lady .niembers have busied themselves. during

the last few months making and sending wool- len comtprts to the soldiers, and various appre- ciative ft ttera have been received from the Front. It May not be out of place to mention also, that the Mission has recently'. furnished and equipped a home for a family, of Belgian refugees, and are providing the Money neces- sary to sustain the family, . which consists of Mother,. two married daughters, a daughter-in- law, and three young Children. As. a Church, we esteem it a privilege and an honour to be able to do something to help that heroic and rely trichexl Imtion, Belgium,

div.head: Past Year Reviewed.
div.p: the Past Year Reviewed.
During the year 1914 we lost three of our I Church members through death—Sister
Hams, Sister Lawson, and Brother. Thomas Taylor. Brother Taylor had occupied the Church Treasurership for close on 20 years, and . _
is difficult to reconcile oneself to his loss.

The various branches of the Mission (Society Class, Christian Endeavour Society, Band of Hope, Rechabite Tents, Children's LanteVn Services, League of Help, &c.) have all done good work during the year, and are looking forward to, and aiming at, a still more successful time during the present year. The Sunday School work has progressed and still entitles the school to the premier position of the Sunday Schools of Warrington, so far as the average attend- ance is concerned. Our friend, Mrs. Crofi field, of Colwyn Bay, has increased our indebt- edness to her during the past twelve months by again defraying the cost of lighting, heating, &c., and by assisting in many other ways, and her valuable help an interest are highly appre- ciated by the workers.

MRS. CROSFIELD'S ADDRESS.

Mrs. John Crosfield, on rising, was greeted• with nnother hearty ovation, and in the course of a sympathetic speech delighted the Belgian refugees by addressing them in their native tongue. After expressing her pleasure at meet- ing those present, Mrs. Crosfield, touching upon the war, said there mtist-be hardly a home in Great Britain that had not been affected by this terrible and cruel war. She was glad to think that they as a nation had been able to show the Belgians some sympathy by receiving them into their homes. She quite agreed with Mr. Parker's remarks about every church and every family that could possibly do so showing the Belgians some hospitality. (Hear, hear.) They could never repay the Belgians as long as they lived for the terrible suffering they had had to endure. It was marvellous the way the Bel- gians had kept up during the last six months. Like the Mission, she had undertaken the care of two Belgian families, consisting of seven people, since last November. (Applause.) They had been placed in a house of hers in Bucking- hamshire. Part of one of the families that lived at Antwerp had been to Holland, and was then brought to England and sent to Derby. Now they were united in the one house, and the re- union was a very happy event One of the wives' brothers was a music hall artiste, with a good voice, and he was now learning English songs, so that he could appear at concerts here. (Hear, hear.) Turning to the wk of the Mission, 'Mrs. ,Crosfield commented upon its very satisfactory nature. They could not at present do anything in the nature of enlarging it, and would have to wait until the end of the war., In conclusion, Mrs Crosfield mentioned the work she was doing in Ireland .for the Royal Irish Fusiliers, and hoped that when' they had time in that Mission they would knit some mittens, socks, &c., for her Dublin boys. (Applause.)

div.head: LANTERN LECTURE ON THE WAR.
div.p: LANTERN LECTURE ON THE WAR.

After the speeches a capital limelight lecture illustrating the progress of the war was given by Mr. Tilling. The slides illustrated Louvain and other now devastated towns in stricken Flanders. The lecture was interspersed with songs rendered by Miss E. Tanner, "Land of Hope and Glory" and "Love's Old Sweet Song," and Mr. E. Pownall, "Boys of the Old, Bri- gade," "Alone in the Desert," and "There's a Land." •

Mr. Arthur Crosfield, . who, with Mrs. Arthur ,Crosfield, arrived late in the 'evening, voiced his thanks to the Mission workers for the re- ception accorded him and his wife, and: also warmly thanked the ladies for the way . they had worked in .connection with the gloves and mittens scheme associated with the Grand Duke Michael's :Committee. •

On the motion of Mr. Thomas Dale a comPre- hensive.A-ote of thanks was heartily passed to Mrs. J. 'Crosfield for presiding; Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Crosfield for honouring the function with their preseifce; the artistes and those who had helped to make the gathering so enjoyable.

div.head: BELGIAN THANKS.
div.p: BELGIAN THANKS.
The Belgians, anxious to indicate their thanks for the hospitality shown them, had also penned the following letter, which was read by Mr. Tilling :

"Ladies and Gentlemen,—The undersigned, still under the impression of the splendid re- ception we received on arrival in Warrington, unanimously beg to thank you all very heartily. -Although we have had to leave our homes and our beloved country, we are happy once more because we have found a new home among you in hospitable England. : "Never will: we forget you when we are once more back in Belgium, which you are nobly re- conquering for us; and may God bless your efforts and that of the Allies in this noble cause. "These and our heartiest thanks we beg you to accept. In the name of us all—(Mrs.) RuCqUoy-Franeks, (Mrs.) Plaquee-Rucquoy, (Mrs.) Rucquoy-Chielemans, and children, Marcel and Suzanne; (Mrs.) Barnich-Rucquoy, and child, Roger. 35, Golborne-street, War- rington. 25th January, 1915." -

div.head: WOMAN'S WORLD.
div.p: WOMAN'S WORLD.
CHAT and .GOSSIP.
By IdARJORIE.

The Flag of Belgium. Not everyone knows the meaning of the Bel- gian flag. The colours signify "Through dark- ness and blood; into the light," and every lover of freedom devoutly hopes that the nation that has- shown such magnificent courage and bravery, will rise phcenix-like from its ashes, to more than its former greatness. A year ago Belgium was a hive of industry, no 'country- in Europe was more prosperous, and its King de- lighted to watch, at close quarters, the develop- ment of the nation's commerce and manufac- tures. In the clothes of a workman he went through big ironworks and down: mines ;he was, in fact, a captain of industry.

King Albert and His Consort. War had been declared but a few days when King Albert assumed another role. He became a soldier, and, in truth, a King. But there is nothing spectacular about him, and never was monarch as democratic as King Albert of Bel- gium, who is indeed the "Lion of Flanders." He rallies his subjects to the fight, and reminds them how their forbears fought for the flag, on many a field, and drove out a foe as strong and cruel as the Germans of to-day. His brave Consort has, by her devotion to the wounded, the sick, and the suffering, made for herself a place in the hearts of the people, just as the valour of her husband has endeared him to his subjects, and aroused the admiration .of the whole world.

div.head: Woman's Influence.
div.p: Woman's Influence.

_ The War Office has made several .appeals to the conscience of the nation, and has asked women not to prevent their menfolk, who are of litili- tary age, from doing their duty by enlisting in the Army. Many' women have behaved with a heroism worthy of the British soldier on the battlefield. They have willingly parted from those near and dear to them, and have worked unremittingly for the .comfort of the troops. But there are others who have dissuaded their sons, brothers and kusbands from enlisting.

Wholemeal Sultana Pudding (for 8 persons).* Into 11b. of wholemeal rub Vb. of butter or nutter, add 11b. currants, 11b. sultanas, 2 level tablespoonfuls sugar, a pinch of salt, and 11 tea- spoonfuls of baking powder, mix with sufficient cold water to form a stiff dough.' Creamed Oysters. One pint of nice oysters, thoroughly drained; one pint of milk, one small tablespoonful of butter, one scant teaspoonful of corn starch, salt and pepper as desired. Heat the milk to boiling, mix butter and corn starch together' and stir in. When boiling add the oysters, which have been brought to a boiling point. Stew altogether until the oysters are well filled out with the edges curling and serve on thin slices of buttered toast or any little dainty salt cracker. To be eaten while hot.

div.p: Japanese Women.

The education of Japanese women has made I extraordinary strides during the last twenty- five year. Only two generations ago, with the exception of the ladies of the highest rank', the women of Japan were altogether illiterate. The only instruction they received, or were sup- posed to require, fitted them for domestic drudges,.but nothing more. Now they are the best educated of all Oriental women. Every village of any size has its excellent elementary school, which the girls enjoy the same advantages as boys. Every town has its high school and _coirtinnation schools. Cleanliness in the Scullery. Careless dish-washing is the indirect, cause of certain forms of illness; fevers, contagious diseases of .the skin, mouth, throa,t and lungs are frequently transmitted .to the wirious members of • a family through dishes- that have been used and then improperly washed and not sterilised. Not infrequently the dishcloths and drying towels' are Used for long periods without. ever being rinsed out in clean, warm water and hung in the sunshine to dry. Dishes should be 'washed in clean, hot water, well soaped. Before commencing. this part of the work, it is advis- able to rinse all food particles from dishes with running water and then.pile the dishes in order around the pan. • Wash glassware and light china and any dishes, that are not .greasy first, and pile them in the rinsing pan; then proceed with the more soiled utensils. When the water becomes greasy it should be changed for clean water. Rinse all dishes except light glassware in boiling water; the latter is a germicide and dishes will he thoroughly disinfected by its use. Glasses, cups, spoons and other 'articles that come in direct contact with the mouth should be kept in boiling water longer than the other dishes so that all danger of possible contamina- tion may be avoided. In luiy 'case dishes used by fever or tubercular patients ..should be scalded thoroughly each -time after -being used. Charles Foxley, a groom-gardener, was charged with wilfully damaging a chair and sofa to the extent of 55., at 182, WeMeld-street, on Monday, and also with obtaining by false pretences foOd and lodging to the value of 65., from Mrs. Ellen Ashurst, a widow. _ _

Mr. CROSFIELD briefly addressed the company. He was glad, he said, to have that chance of thanking so many of the most active workers for the admirable help they had given in pro- viding so many useful garments, as well as a large stock of exqellent mittens for the soldiers. The outbreak of war did not find England in a state of preparedness to the. extent of having been •ready to cope with a move that would plunge Europe into such a seething cauldron. was told in London only last . week that Germany had ,t 25,000,000 worth of ammunition ready before this war, whilst he understood that a mere fraction of that large sum would cover the cost of all that Britain, Russia and France had got between them. He thought they would appreciate the bearing a fact like that. had upon the assertion that poor Germany had had the present war thrust upon her. (Laughter.) Still, although Britain was not prepared to that ex- tent, it was utterly inaccurate and a very great mistake to talk as if we were altogether unpre- pared. (Hear, hear.) They had done a great deal to prepare themselves for eventualities, but they had done it along normal lines. They were not,prepared for the abnormal, And natur- ally when it was decided that besides our vast Naval power, our unrivalled striking. force for service overseas, and our gallant Territorials— when it was decided that we must produce an enormous and powerfully equipped army to form the deciding factor in this mighty contest, why, then, naturally, there was a great deal to be provided in the way of clothing, of munitions of war, of uniforms and boots, of under-cloth- ing, and ever so much besides. There was no doubt that the War Office in London had--as

was admitted on all hands—grappled wonder- fully with an enormously difficult task. (Hear, hear.) But they could not foresee everything, nor could they get evewthing done at once, and, among other things, those very humble, but very comforting and most necessary articles Which the Liberal women of Warrington were working so hard. to make, were, he was afraid, rather overlooked. He wits glad to say that what was needed had now to. a large extent been provided. Lord Kitchener wanted 500,000 pairs of gloves and mittens, and so far—thanks to the efforts that had been put forth by busy and enthusiastic ladies throughout the country —he had been able to send 300,000 pairs to the Front. (Applause.) He did not think that it required any great stretch of the imagination to realise what a great boon, and indeed what a GOdsend, that vast quantity of necessary com- forts, and of comfortable necessaries, must have been to our men through this cold winter weather. (Applause.) Splendid work had been done by the Liberal women, and, also, he was glad to say, by women of every shade of political opinion in Warrington, to see to it that the old' town did its share in -ministering' to the needs of our men at the Front. (Hear, hear.)

ner in which their soldiers and sailors had re- sponded to the call of the highest patriotism. It did them all good to reflect on the self-sacrificing ardour with which our men on the high seas and across the Channel were fighting this great battle for England, for the Empire; yes, and for the entire civilised world. They could not think of the great deeds that were making history to- day without a patriotic glow of pride in the heart of every young lady in Warrington, and in the heart of every lady who might not be quite so young—(laughter)—who had taken a share in the splendid work being carried on in that building toP provide our brave fellows with,. as he had put it, those necessaries which were comforts, and comforts which were nec4saries„ to aid them in their task. On his Wife's behalf, as well as his own, he was very glad to have had the opportunity that evening of tendering. thanks to the Liberal lady workers of Warring- ton for the splendid amount of work they had done for the benefit of our gallant soldiers. (Hear, hear.) If they wanted .to discover some of the grounds upon 4vhich, he submitted, they had reason to hope that long before another Christmas came -round the present hiteful and scandalous war would be ended, he ventured to suggest that they should keep their eyes on some of the political developments that were not unlikely to take place in the course of the next few months. It was not for nothing that, apart from the magnificent army they had re- cruited in this country, and in other parts of the Empire, there were 600,000 very able fighting men in Roumania on the pant of coming in. (Applause.) Moreover, only a week since he attended a deeply interesting meeting in Lon- don, at which it was made abundantly manifest that the Greeks, to a man, were with the Allies. (Applause.) The Greek Minister in London made a speech at that meeting, which had been reported in the Press all over Europe. The speech was really a most significant declaration, and it seemed to point to the fact that they were fast Approaching a time when Germany' would find that she had scarcely one solitary friend left among the nations of the world. Could she expect to have what she had so utterly failed to deserve? When they read of the deliberate advice given by the German General Staff to its officers; when they read their' Manual of Instructions, the cold-blooded in- famy, the calculated and deliberate brutality, bestiality, and barbarism of it all, they began to wonder how much further the neutral nations of the world would permit this kind of thing to go; how much longer the most solemn obligations of international treaties were to lab ignored, and, in fact, these treaties torn to shreds and tatters. (Applause.) Not the least serious mistake Germany had made, as she would discover, had been in the way of opening the eyes of the neutral nations to the fact that she stood committed to a policy which, in its ' essence, was nothing more or less than an at- tempt to plunge the whole of Europe back into the dark ages of barbarism. But the attempt would not be allowed to succeed. (Applause.)

played in encouraging their menfolk to go and do their duty by the old. country and by the great Empire, whose traditions were such a priceless heritage to the people of these islands. (Applause.) To-day men and women could not meet to- gether without thinking about the war. They could not go into any, circle of society without hearing the war talked about, and the main question, about which everybody was speculat- ing, was as to how long the fighting is going to last. Speaking in Warrington, he was optimis- tic enough to assert that the talk they had heard of a war that would be dragged out for between two and three years was much too pessimistic an estimate to the probabilities of the • situa- tion. Although there was not a man in Europe who could pretend. to make any tFue prediction as to the date of the end of the war, he, nevertheless, felt that they had very good grounds for confidently hoping that, at the very latest, between August and October next would see the whole sad business finished. (Hear, hear.) There were even grounds for hop- ing that June or July might see the end. The work in the way of recruiting and training men, which was proceeding apace in this country, was beyond all praise. It was magnificent. It was as fine as the spirit in which the men were going to the Front. (Applause.) div.p: "A Bit of a Staggerer for the Fatherland."
Mr. CROSFIELD said that it gave Mrs. Crosfield and him the greatest possible pleasure to be thgre and meet so many good friends from the Wilitecross Ward. lie was very glad, too, to

' have the opportunity of thanking the ladies ' from the ward who, in connection with the Women's Liberal, Association had done so much good 'work in the way of turning out useful garments to add to the comfort and health of the soldiers at the Front. They were all enor- mously proud of the splendid spirit of • the British fighting men. (Hear, hear.) The men of this country had come forward in .a way that had Wade some people, On 'the Continent shiver .more than a little as they thought of the tenacity of the British bull-dog. He wanted that night particularly to refer to a fact which they must , never forget, and that was, that the women of England, in more ways than...one, had • played, and were playing, a great part in the tremendous struggle that was - taking place. Men might do the fighting, lint equipment. was half of the battle; and that was where the ladies came in. The spirit and the industry of the 'women of England had been magnificent. No man .could make a bigger sacrifice than many. women had been called upon to make— the *omen Who sat at home and encouraged those they loved best to go and sacrifice, if need be, their lives, and, at any rate, to run the risk of ,doing so. The women of England had played a' splendid and patriotic part in that respect. (Applause.)

He ventured: to. point out the importance, of providing the soldiers .with the articles, re- quired; pointed., out, in fat, that the difference between warm- hands and a good blood-Circula- tion and hands, that were chilled and numbed by the bitter elements, might mean all the dif- ference" between a man saving his life and losing it. The response to the appeal he ,made had been kind and generous. Thanks to the work done in Warrington, and in so many other towns, as well as in the country districts up and down the land, Lord Kitchener had been enabled to send over 300,000 pairs of gloves and mittens to the Front. It was unnecessary to emphasise- the value to the men at the Front of that huge consignment of useful articles. (Hear, hear.) It was a big task that was set the women of England, and he thanked the women of Warrington for the part they had taken in it. (Applause.) The previous night he had had a few words to say in that hall about the duration of the war, and lie said that there was no 'man in Europe who could say when it was going to end. It was true that there was no such man, but he was, that night, going to be very rash and to make the predic- tion and give them a tip—a tip they could put their money on if they liked—tlaughter)— though, of course, in the presence of the twn's Chief Magistrate and Mayor, .he would not, for the life of him, say a word calculated to en- courage gambling or betting. (Renewed laugh- ter.) He was only giving them a quiet little tip. When the time ,came for terms to be men- tioned to Germany, he expected the people of this country, and of the ,nations allied with. them, would see for a few weeks, or; possibly, for a few months,' a series of convulsive efforts on the part of the foe, because the terms that would be dictated would, to say the least of them, be a little bit of a staggerer for the Fatherland. (Hear, hear.)
BITTER PILL IN STORE FOR GERMANY.

They would, in fact, be terms such as would constitute a very bitter pill for the Germans `to swallow. But in spite of the bitterness, to them, of the terms, the Germans, who, after all, were a very' instructed people—and it was the very fact of their education that ought to cover them with the more abyssmal shame for all that they had made themselves responsible —would say to themselves: "Certainly, to accept those terms is for us a disaster, and a disaster on an enormous scale; but, to go on fighting and running our heads against a stone wall can, in the end, only mean annihilation, and we. prefer disaster to that." He hoped his hearers would not think that in saying that he was making a very rash kind of prophecy. He trusted that before' many months were over they would. be seeing the, end of the terrific war, and that when the end did come it would be accompanied by a sgttlement based upon nation- ality; by such a 'settlement 'as would make it out of --the question for such a European Armageddon to ever be repeated in history. (Hear, hear.) It was said that history some- times repeated itself, and so it very often did. but, mercifully, for the sake of poor humanity, it did net always repeat itself. They had seen no repetition, nor would they ever see a repeti- tion, of the North and South War in America— that terrible conflict that took place in the time of the Lanashire cotton famine; only too well remembered in the County ;Palatine.. IThat awful civil war took' place between 1860 and 1864„ and it had been calculated that, from start to finish, it involved the loss of nearly a million lives. It was one of the most terrible 'things known in history, and it would,,never he repeated. SINISTER RACE PROBLEMS AHEAD.

He did not wish to be understood as saying that when the present terrible conflict was over they would have reached the Millennium, in the matter of warfare, for there were sad and sinister problems still ahead of humanity, pro- blems embracing the great race question of the world—the great colour question of the races af the East and the West, concerning which they might hope for wise guidance to steel Humanity's Ship of State safely through the difficult waters. Still, without prophesyin. that, with the close of the present war, they would see the end of all great wars, they did hope that the nations of the West would worl; together for the avoidance of a repetition of th 4 gikantic struggle now in progress, to the end that the great, educated white races would never again, throughout the whole course of history, tolerate a European Armageddon. That thought must be in the minds and hearts of the seldiers who were fighting in the ranks 'of the Allies :ma of the tens and hundreds of thousands- in this. country who were getting ready to put the finishing touches to the struggle. The men of England who had joined up were doing their duty to their, 'country in a conflict which, from the point of view of' its consequences and its influence on future history,, would be in every sense of the word the vasteq. the greatest and the most righteous struggle that this nation had over engaged in-. Several of the parents, who attendi.d the Court, said they could not understand what had made their boys act as they did. " WAITING " IN THE CEMETERY.

Last week, in this column, we drew attention to a complaint we had received respecting the arrangement by which one clergyman in turn officiates at all funerals in the Ceme- tery on a given date. The I,F,CTOR. (the Rev. CANON WILLIS) writes us on the subject as follows

I have read Your article on the Funerals at the Cemetery in to-day's " Examiner." There is another side to the question. The present arrangement is the result of my proposals some twenty years ago. When I came, the Incumbents of the various parishes took their own funerals. The result was that sometimes. there were five or six clergy spending an hour or more a day where one man could have done the work properly and reverently in a quarter of the time. I know that under the. present system there is the dis- advantage of the . clergyman not knowing the mourners in many cases, but the clergy are always willing to take any particular funeral when specially desired. Of course, there is also on some occasions delay, -for which, I am sure, we are very sorry, but the officiating clergyman shares it to the full. ,

"A NONCONFORMIST," who goes some- what into detail, sends us this contri- bution on the subject of "Cemetery Reform" I read with interest your leader upon one of the unnecessary discomforts which attaches to our local burial system. May I point out that Nonconformists also suffer inconvenience under the existing usage, though not, perhaps, in the same way? It is the rule that funerals of Dis- senters shall take place at 2.30 on week-Clays and 2on SundSys. Where four or five funerals are arranged for one day and are timed to arrive at the same moment it is obvious that all cannot enter the chapel at once. The last arrivals must wait until the others have passed through the chapel, and as the service lasts from fifteen to twenty minutes in each case, a period of unhappy waiting must be endured. When attending a funeral not long ago we were told that the Cemetery Chapel was held by members of a sect who usually sang a few hymns and delivered addresses, and whose tenure of the chapel could not be estimated with any cer- tainty.- In despair of gaining possession of the chapel, the minister read the service out of doors. Fortunately the winter day was mild; but what if the weather had been of the worst?

The remedy is surely very simple. Could not a, time be suggested by the Registrar which would avoid crowding and confusion? If one funeral is to be at 2.30, could not 2.15 and 2.45 be. fixed as the times for any two others which fell upon the same day? And, for the matter of that, why fix 2.30 at all? Why not give the bereaved family the choice of time at any hour, say, between 12 and 4? The convenience of those who travel long distances to attend a funeral, and who desire to return the same day, ought surely to be considered. Such an exten- sion of burial hours would require no increase in the Cemetery staff; but it would, on the other hand, do much to relieve the pressure which falls upon the Registrar and his .assistants in the crowded hour between 2.30 and 3.30.

Incidentally, would it not be an advantage to funeral furnishers? It is an open secret that the shortage of men and horses caused- by the war has put them in a dilemma, and an arrange- ment which enabled them to use carriages for two funerals upon the same day (a thing im- possible under the present plan) would be.very gratefully welcomed. This criticism is not intended to reflect upon the conduct of the Cemetery officials, whose courtesy and co-operation under difficult cir- cumstances is all that could be desired.

It will be remembered. that we did not blame anyone for the cause of com- plaint that has undoubtedly arisen. All we asked was that the Cemetery arrangements should be reviewed in the light of experience gained over -a long number of Years, during which conditions, in many directions, have changed. The letters of both our valued corregpondents prove, we think, the reasonableness of that suggestion.

div.p: VICAR OF *ST. PETER'S ADVICE.

The Rev. B. Percival, speaking at St. Peter's parochial tea party on Monday night, called attention to the danger of treating soldiers with strong drink. They would have seen from the local papers, he said, the sad result of treating the men on duty at the Walton Swing Bridge at the New Year. A man had given them a bottle of whisky and a woman had given them beer, with the consequence that an assault was made upon the policeman on duty, who might have been shot, and the men had been dis- graced. This, doubtless, was the work of thoughtless people, for he could not bring him- self to believe that it was done with intent to do harm, but the,consequence was very serious for the men, and might have been tragic. He pleaded with them thai on no account should they give strong drink. They might give cigar- ettes or tobacco if, they would; that would not muddle the brain and cause them to lose self- control. Chocolate was rather a nice present to give a soldier, and he would be delighted to receive it. The very safety of the country de- pended upon the fitness of our men, and not only should we place no temptation in their way, but we should do our utmost to remove every temptation out of their way. "Let us lay this matter to heart," coneluded the reverend gentleman.

div.head: 'EARLY CLOSING OF PUBLIC-HOUSES
div.p: 'EARLY CLOSING OF PUBLIC-HOUSES
For Stockton Heath and Neighbouring Places.

At a meeting of the Licensing Justices of the Dansbury Division of Cheshire, held on Tues- day at the office of the Clerk, Mr. Henry Greenall, , Warrington, it was decided to put into operation the Intoxicating Liquors (Tem- porary Restriction) Act, which means that the public-houses in the division %lin, presumably for the period of the war, be opened later and closed oaxlier than is the custom.

Several .efforts had already been made to in- duce (the justices to apply the Act, but in vain. Since the treating of the guards at Walton lariage 'caned marked attention to a scandalous State of affairs, Colonel Malcolm, Chief Con- stable of the County, again took action, and it was the recommendation of Colonel Malcolm that came" before the justices on Tuesday. We understand that the magistrates agreed by only a small majority. The result, however, will be that the licensed houses in the division will in future be opOn as follows:— Week-days, froth 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Sundays, from 12.30 p.m. to 2.30 p.m. from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. The present hours are : Week-days, from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. Sundays, from 12.30 p.m. to 2.30 p.m. from 6 p.m. to 10 p.m.
The change will come into operation a fort- night from the day of the decision—that is, a week next Tuesday. _ _

The following place' are in the Daresbury Division and will be under the new Order:— Stockton Heath, Latchford Without, Walton, Daresbury, Whitley, Antrobus, Grappenhall, Appleton, Moore, Dutton, Stret ton, Acton Grange, Partington, Hatton, Keckwick, Newton- by-Daresbury, Preston-o'-th'-Hill, and Seven- oaks.

div.head: LOCAL FEELING.
div.p: LOCAL FEELING.

The matter has been the subject of much comment in, the districts named, and; as is common in such things, our representative found that opinions differed upon the advisa- bility or otherwise of restricting the hours. Those in favour of the new order, and they are numerous, admit that as far as "scones in the street" through drink are concerned, the new hours will not bring about any material change, but they contend that decreased facilities for spending money on drink are bound to have a beneficial effect in the homes of the people. The Rev. G. Curtis (Hill Cliff° Baptik Church) said he would most heartily, welcome any reduction of the hours in which drink could be bought. This was a time when clear think- ing and clean living was most essential to the manhood of the nation, if good soldiers were to be produced to end this terrible war. A man soaked in beer, or suffering from its evil effects, was not the kind of soldier or sailor that would win battles. How very necessary it was that all temptation should. be put aside was conclusively proved by the action of Russia in prohibiting the sale of vodka, and of France in tabooing absinthe. Muddled heads and wrecked consti- tutions would not bring the present crisis to a speedy termination, nor would they help those who stay at home to bear the misfortune of bereavement or reverses that must come in a titanic struggle such as we were going through now. The only way to promote sobriety was to decrease the opportunities for drinking. He had not the slightest doubt that the inhabitants of the Daresbury Division ,would, as time went on, feel the benefit of this new restriction. Every hour less passed in the public-house meant more money for the wife and children at home, and it also meant better health and an improved moral outlook on life. He noticed that other divisions in Cheshire had already adopted "restricted hours," and was glad to think that the good they had derived would shortly be shared by the Daresbury Division.

div.head: DEAF-EARS OF "THE TRADE.-
div.p: THE DEAF-EARS OF "THE TRADE.-
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—The thanks of this town and district are due to you for your timely editorial in last Saturday week's issue of "The Examiner." No domestic incidents have pained the community more than the sight of drunken and semi- drunken soldiers. You very justly censure the foolish people who supplied drink to the soldiers on duty at Walton Bridge. The cruelty of some kindnesses has no language for descrip- tion. To tempt soldiers on or off duty is not only anti-patriotic; it is treason. But when we have finished with the people who foolishly are the soldiers'. worst enemies, what should he said of the trade that makes such an act possible? What should be said of magistrates who consider there is no reason to interfere with the normal sale of liquor? When an appeal is made to "The Trade" it is made unto deaf. ears. No national crisis, no national need, no national righteousness, appeals to its love of gain. Soldiers have been drunk, soldiers have been disorderly, soldiers have disgraced their uniforms and regiments all through drink. France prohibits the sale of liquor. Russia, backward Russia, as we say in England, wipes her hands of it, but "The Trade" here has pushed "Business as usual," in spite of Lord Kitchener and his noble sister. The voice of the dead leader, Lord Roberts, has even no influence.

Punish those who foolishly supply drink to soldiers or sailors we ought; but the nation should inflict a national castigation upon such as nurture our Army and Navy with one hand and curse the men, body, soul and mind, with the other.
Surely, sir, after the able lead of your paper, Warrington ought to set herself right on this question, and also remember that your able
Continued in next Column.
FOOD PRICES.
Shipping Freights And The Shipowners' Harvest. ACTION DEMANDED.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—Nothing could more strikingly show the absurdity of our economic system than our help- lessness regarding the many rises in food prices, which, so far, the British householders have faced with remarkable cheerfultiess. The posi- tion is daily growing worse, and is bringing into many thousands of poor homes anxiety as to how to make both ends meet. Unfortunately, there is no prospect of any fall in the prices. However, we British householders have in many ways very much to be thankful for— thanks to our Navy, which, of sourse, is main- tained by us, and is certainly justifying every farthing spent on it—but, perhaps, it should be remembered that there are limits to our endur- ance at such a crisis as the present, especially when we know that many individuals are out for their "pile," and are making it, not caring who pays. But who does pay? Only the poor. Why should food prices be so sensationally high? There is no shortage. In the Argen- tine they have had a splendid harvest. The merchants are not asking a sensational price for their produce. The chief reason lies in the ex- traordinary increase in the cost of freights. For instance, freight for grain from the Argentine to Liverpool has risen from 11s. to 625. per ton, equal to over 400 per cent. increase. Who is taking the " extra "? The shipowners. The shipowners are at present having a good time, or, to use the words of Mr. Stoker, the chairman of the Manchester Liners, which he recently gave to a Press representative,." Ship- owners are certainly making good returns," whilst the "huge public investment" is keeping the seas clear, for the shipowners to feed the nation at their own price, and the poor people, the dependents of those men who are gallantly fighting for us, both on land and sea, are paying a great deal more for the means of "living." Does it not strike you as disgraceful that such a state of affairs should be allowed to pro- ceed, at such a crisis as this, especially when the Government has the power to take the necessary steps to regulate the freightage, or better still, nationalise shipping, as well as the railways? The German Government would not allow their shipowners to act ill this way at a time like this. It should be remembered the Government already have commandeered nearly 2,000 ships for their own use, so that They have full power to intervene and regulate the rates, or pur- chase the ships, and at their own price. The public think they are dealing with a vast " army " of shipowners—certainly there are a great number of shipping houses, with different names and "flags "—and that competition should enable a " regulation" of rates. Not so, the merchant /service is full of "rings," there- fore, owners are able to fix, in conference, their own figure what the shipper shall pay-, and must pay. It is also worth recalling that at the com- mencement of the war the Government specially fixed prices for foodstuffsraritig the months of August and September, but now no lists are published at all, especially when the day is no brighter, but more "dullish." We will hope that the Government will step in and put an end to a disgraceful business. Yours faithfully, PETER PEArOCK, JUN. sankey, Warrington, January 22, 1915.

When the Warrington Infirmary was extended a few years ago at a cost representing the greater part of £20,000, it was found that the available funds would not allow of the furnishing and, maintenance of all the three large added wards. Local Leather Trade. "Trade," writes the Warrington correspon- dent of the "Leather Trades Review," "pre- sented few changed features last week; matters were running smoothly, with a ready opening for most of the goods as they came along. The only complaint is that deliveries are too slow, ' but as the contributing cause is one over which tanners have small control, they can only regret it and hope for more suitable weather. The demand for Army lines is as brisk as ever; any- thing near requirements is readily taken up, and as nearly every class of bends is called upon, either by the boot or accoutrement maker, this section moves very strongly. Stout shoulders and bellies are in very good demand, and satisfactory prices are willingly paid. Strap butts, too, are in better inquiry, but offers are comparatively small, and, when business results prices show an advance of about 50 per cent. on ante-war prices. The purely domestic trade IS quiet, and makes but small demands on the market, but repairers are very busy, and ac- count for a considerable quantity of leather. There is little change of values to record, and tanners have generally no difficulty in fully Isaintaining prices, which are regarded as fairly axed for a time; for proopt or forward delivery both sellers and buyers ars operating confidently IA this bask"

Extending a welcome to the men to attend ser- vice at the churches and chapels, he said men experienced some difficulty in the midst of worry and business to attend the services of the sanc- tuary. They say they need some lighter pleas- ures and amusements as a recreation from the close duties of business. They contend that churches and chapels are for men .aifti women who have little to do. Th9,4r excuses are weak when looked at from fhe great ideals of Christ and His teaching. He, the great Prophet, lived a life of toil and service for man and God. In setting our minds upon God and His great will we shall have greater power in business and worldly pursuits. div.head: Facts About the Force.
div.p: Facts About the Force.

During last year, states the Chief Constable, in his annual report, the Warrington police, among their other multifarious duties, restored to their parents 274 children, who were found wandering in the streets, and conveyed to the pinfold 52 horses, cattle, sheep, &c., found straying on the highway. In the same period they seized 293 stray dogs, of which number 116 were destroyed, 41 sold and 136 restored to their owners. In 1913, 381 dogs were seized. The police rendered assistance in 103 collisions and atcidents caused by runaway horses, &c., and conveyed 605 persons (463 males and 142 females) to lI.M. prisons at Liverpool and Manchester. In addition they arrested 26 prisoners of WM.: and took them to camps at Queensferry, New- bury and Handiorth. During the year 444 articles were found and deposited at the police office. Of that number 253 were !restored to their owners, seven were returned to the finders, and the remaining 184 are still unclaimed. The occupants of 202 houses intimated their inten- tion of leaving their residences unoccupied at different periods, and the police gave extra supervision to such residences day and night. No fewer than 1,588 informations from other police forces, describing property stolen and persons wanted were inquired into, with the re- sult that in several instances the property had been recovered and the thieves arrested. The number of ex-members of the borough constabu- lary who are on the pension fund is 22, viz., two who were chief inspectors, two who were inspec- tors, eight who were sergeants, one who was an acting-sergeant and nine who! were constables. div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
BRILLIANT. MUSICAL PLAY AT THE ROYAL COURT.
Since _Christmas frequenters of the Royal

Court Theatre have been privileged to see, hear and enjoy three musical plays of an exception- ally high standard of interest. "The Dollar Princess," which is being presented this week, is in many respects the best of this trio of good things. While its scenery and costumes, its action and incident, do not, perhaps, outshine the others, it is,;musidally, a long way ahead of them. Mr. Leo Fall has brought distinct originality of thought to bear in clothing the novel theme of tlii) play with music in which brightness and an overflowing Vifaciousness are always in pleasurable evidence. The score is something very much more than the usual string of loosely-hanging musical trifles, and the orchestration bears the impress of the master hand. But for the interpolation of spoken vi[ords, and the inclusioß of some well-nigh in- *minable gag, for which the librettist can hardly be held regponsible, the music almost lifts the play into the exalted ranks of grand opera. This superiority of the music is at once seen in the connectedness of its numbers and the free use that is made in the score of recita- tive mid lyrical dialogue. Several ensemble pieces, in which the parts for principal and choral voices are closely knit together, and which run to considerable length, are full of charm, and two of these give an intensity of interest to finales which it is now, alas! quite .unusual to find in works of this class. Messrs. Macdon- ald and Young's company is an excellent one in an all-round sense, and with a superb stage set- ting to back them up, the rdeMbers of it prescn:ed the play with dashing brilliance and verve. With no desire to make invidious distinctions, one feels impelled to record the conspicuous suc- cesses in both singing and acting of Miss Nancy - Gibbs as Alice, Miss Maud Underwood as Olga, Mr. Martin Iredale as Fairfax, and Mr. Charles Midgeley as Condor. And, associated with these, a' special word of praise is due to Mr. Alfred Clarke for his inimitable portrayal of the droll part of Bulger, with its attendant group of more or less topical songs. As will be gathered from what has been said of the music, upon the orchestra much of the success of "The Dollar Princess" depends. It is due to my that, a little unsteady during the earlier nights, the bandsmen pulled together admirably under the skilful conductorship of Mr. Albert Vernon, as the week ran its length. Needless to add, that large houses have ruled during the six perform- ances given up to last evening, and .that de- lighted audiences have, during each presenta- tion, shown their high appreciation of the play's sparkling qualities in a most unequivocal way. For the comfort of the numerous patrons of Sir Joseph Beecham's well-conducted theatre and the smoothness with which all activities run therein, a large share of the credit must be given to Mr. H. L. Warburton, the ever-genial and courteous acting-manager.

div.head: TIIRILLS, FUN AND MUSIC AT THE
div.p: TIIRILLS, FUN AND MUSIC AT THE
HIPPODROME.

Du Callon is the "bright, particular star" . , in an excellent programme at the Hippodrome this week. His show is an extremely novel and daring one. Perched in giddy fashion on the rungs of a tall, ladder, which he balances in a bewildering manner on a small platform in the centre of the stage, he keeps up a running fire of witticisms, and, ever and anon, sends cold shudders down the backs of his audience by talking of the sickening thud" that would be heard if he toppled over into the stalls. Whilst aloft on his unstable perch he performs many acrobatic feats, and, generally speaking, gives a performance that cannot fail to satiate even the most ardent lover of. thrills. Arthur Ferriss pays another welcome visit to War- rington, his comedy character studies in song being as delightful as ever. The one depicting the "joys" of the "open road," as viewed from the standpoint of the professional tramp, is quite a work of art in its particular line. The Baits—a trio of Belgian artistes, whose home at Antwerp was among the buildings destroyed by the German Shells—are responsible for some wonderful wire-Walking and acrobatic work, their concluding feat being especially clever and daring. "My Fancy," a dainty young lady dancer, gives an altogether delightful turn, en- titled "A Study in Black and White," presum- ably, by reason of the fact that her costumes and the stage appointments are solely in thoSe colours. Rowland, described on the programme as "the brainstorm , juggler," is wonderfully dexterous and invests his performance with much novelty, whilst Penman,and Miller add to the attractiveness of their smart gymnastic work by introducing a vein of genuine comedy. An excellent vocal turn is provided by the Snaefells—"Manxland's representative singers" —and Walter Lawley and Sadie East appear in an attractive musical comedietta, into which they introduce a clever satire on the manners and fashions of to-day, yesterdaf; and ,the day before: They are a really 'smart pair. This week's issue of "The Gaumont Graphic" in- cludes pictures showing the damage. wrought during the recent -German air raid on Yar- mouth and King's Lynn. Taken all round, this week's show is a thoroughly enjoyable one and no lover of varieties should miss it.

div.head: Next Week's Attractive Bill.

div.p: UNITED STATES OF EUROPE.
A Wished-For Outcome of the War. BOLD STREET WESLEY GUILD FESTIVAL.

Great success attended the annual Guild Festival in connection with the Bold-street Wes- leyan Church, which was held on Sunday and Monday. The special preacher on the first day was the Rev. Thomas Miller (formerly of the Warrington Circuit), and he also gave .an ad- dress to the Guilders and their friends on Monday. In the course of his Sunday morning sermon Mr. Miller said that although it was often said and often written that the present war had come upon the nations of Europe like "a bolt from the blue," that was not really the case, because long before the assassination of the Archduke Ferdinand supplied Germany with a' " casus belli," trouble had . been brewing in many other directions. Special music was rendered at both the morn- ing and evening services. At the former the choir gave "0, for a closer walk with God," whilst in the evening their anthem was "By Babylon's wave." Mr. F. Hickman presided at the organ at both services, and the solo part of the anthem in the morning was taken by Miss E. Taylor.

div.head: "VAR AND OUR IDEALS."
div.p: "VAR AND OUR IDEALS."
Germany's Embittered State-
Consciousness.

The Rev. Thomas Miller's address on the Mon- day evening was entitled "The War and Our Ideals," and it was listened to by a large attend- ance, over whom Mr. F. Harris presided. By way of prelude to his address, Mr. Miller paid a tribute to the work of the Wesley Guilds, which, he said, provided a splendid means for the training of ChUrchworkers. Turning to the war, he said that they rejoiced as English men and women that at the present juncture their ineerests and their conceptions of honour coin- cided. Had it been otherwise one wondered what would have happMied, although one was entitled to believe and to hope, judging from the past history of this country, that the nation would have—as it had done—risen to the height required of it, though one could not help admit- ting that throughout the discussion which pre- Ceded the war there was constant reference to "our" interests." "What should be the atti-

tucte of the Christian concerning this war?" was an oft reiterated question, and there were a few Christians who had gone so far as to say that in • harmony with what was understood to be the teaching of the Sermon on the Mount, this country ought not to have offered active resist- ance, but should have allowed the Germans to engage in warfare if they thought fit, and not to have taken part in it itself. •
MUST USE THE ORDINARY WEAPONS OF THE NATION.

He could not, see eye to eye With that section of the Christian Church, for, to his mind, God made use of national instincts and national life, and, although there were passages in the Bible which they still held .before them as tpe ideal—passages about not resisting evil and tuiln- ing the cheek to the smiter—he believed that, since the national life should be really recog- nised, they must take their place and use one of the ordinary weapons of the nation to defend their honour. At the same time he did not believe that that was the highest conception; nor did he believe it was the way by which God would always have them advance His kingdom, but he did believe that it was the only possibility at the present moment. Looking at the war from the German standpoint, they could readily understand how that nation had arrived at 'their present position. Their own history favoured their conception, for their State had been built up by short, sharp and successful wars. As to-day, so in the past, the Germans had not scrupled about breaking treaties. On the one side of them they had Russia, wham they regarded as a menace, and on the other .side of their frontier was France smarting under a sense of wrong which had existed ever since the Franc4Prussian War; the result being that German State-conscious- ness had been developed with a sense of bitter- ness—the theory of the survival of the fittest had been translated. ruthlessly into the State- life of the country.

div.head: SOLDIER MUST NOT BE MADE THE TYPE.
div.p: THE SOLDIER MUST NOT BE MADE THE TYPE.

One question with the people of this country in these days of militarism was to see that, whilst they regarded the soldier with due honour, they did not advance him as the type of citizenship and did not set up the military state as their ideal of the Kingdom of Christ. He had a profound admiration for soldiers, but he would not like England to be under the power of the military element. It would be a bad day for this country if, in freeing itself from Prus- sian militarism, it allowed a system of a like kind t& be established within its own shores.

As Christians, they stood for the brotherhood of the race and a federation of the nations. They did not believe that Germans, British and French were, by the will of God, purposed to be in eternal antagonism. One prayed that even out of this conflict there would come a United States of Europe. Unless that did transpire, it would be mere rhetorlt to talk about this war ending war. Permanent peace would never be ecured until the manufacture of armaments, ammunition, and of everything relating to war became the exclusive property of the State.

div.head: IF MIGHT IS NOT RIGHT –
div.p: IF MIGHT IS NOT RIGHT -

There was another aspect of the question of war, and that was that if might was not right when applied to. German methods, it should not be so in English industrial life. The trade union, because it might have the grip of the throat of the employer, must not tyrannise; and the employer, because he had the control of the cupboard of the employe, must not tyrannise either. He did not think that the world would ever bathe same as it was before the war. When men of all grades of society had met in the trench and in the barrack-room, a great leaven- ing of society would take place. The men would understand the masters better, and the masters would see the value of men more, because they had realised the nobility which had prompted _them to such a great sacrifice. The young man who to-day made his career the first considera- tion ought to be ashamed of himself. The first consideration was that at all costs this Country .must win, and the cause of righteousness must prevail. On the proposition of the Rev. H. Williamson a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the lec- turer.

div.head: BANK MEETINGS.
div.p: BANK MEETINGS.
How the Credit of the World Was Saved.
PARR'S BANK, LIMITED.
At the 50th ordinary general meeting of Parr's Bank, Ltd., in London, on Thursday, Mr. Cecil F. Parr presided over a large 'attendance of shareholders, who included Mr. Robert Pier- point.

The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report and the declaration of a dividend of 18 per cent. for the 'half-year, subject to income tax (making 19 per cent. for the year), detailed the unprecedented position in financial matters caused by the sudden outbreak of the war. The prompt measures -taken by the Government, who very wisely (riled in the advice and co- operation of representative banking and finan- cial authorities, at once steadied the nerves both of the city and the country. It was highly creditable to the public that the Treasury notes issued to meet the crisis had been so readily szcented. The Government saved the situation, ar by thus successfully supporting English credit, may be said to have saved and main- tained the fabric of credit throughout the civilised world. It was greatly to the credit of the Government that in devising,.these schemes for the relief of the various interests which were threatened, they took full advantage of. the 'in- formation and experience placed at their dis- posal by banking and other experts, whose special knbwledge of the problems to be solved proved of the greatest value. Their general manager, Mr. Whalley, had been an active mem- ber of various committees of bankers which had met very frequently in order to assist in meeting the unparalleled situation created by the war. It would be a bold man who at- tempted to prophesy the immediate future of banking profits. With the continuance of hos- tilities, the needs of the war, and the slackness of trade, other than industries ministering to the needs of the war, everything pointed to the desirability of a cautious view, and the husband- ing of the resources of the bank for the present. He thought to be able to pay comfortably a dividend of 19 per cent. in all the circumstances reflected nothing but credit on the manage- ment. (Applause.) The report was adop-rd, and .the customary elections were made.

div.head: LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE.
div.p: LANCASHIRE AND YORKSHIRE.

Mr. Thomas B. Moxon, presiding over the annual meeting of this bank, at Manchester yes- terday, moved the adoption of the report. He said that in face of all the difficulties of the year they had been able to make provision for all bad and doubtful debts in the same liberal manner as they had always done, they had added £5,000 to the reserve fund, and they recommended a dividend of 16s. per share, sub- ject to income tax. They were increasing the amount carried forward. by £6,000. There was a gratifying increase in the number of cus- tomers, notwithstanding the state of affairs, and it was specially satisfactory to note that ever since the war started there had been ,an addi- tion to their number nearly every week. He was no prophet, but he was not pessimistic in his views of the future. It was lamentable that so many lives and so much money should be wasted in this horrible carnage, but the re- sources of the world were enormous, and with the return of peace they should in a very few years make up for the losses that all nations, combatants and neutrals alike, had sustained through the war. The report (a copy of which has already ap- peared in "The Examiner ") was adopted,- and the election of directors, &c., was proceeded with. Replying to a vote of thanks, _ . _ .
The Chairman said that during the past six months not a moment of his time had he de- voted to anything but the bank's interests.

div.head: LONDON, CITY AND MIDLAND. Gold Reserve In Germany.
div.p: LONDON, CITY AND MIDLAND. Gold Reserve In Germany.

Sir Edward Holden, who presided at the general meeting of the above bank in London, yesterday, reviewed the methods by which the Germans have provided for their war charges, and said the new loan of 250 million sterling for financing the war would be obtained from the Reischbank, which would carry on the war for another six months. Then more funds would be required, when new loans would be issued, and further properties pledged, so they might expect an evil day when this huge pledging will have to be paid off. The question arose how often this operation could be repeated, while there was no doubt that the exports of Germany. would fall off to a much greater extent than her imports, which would have to be paid for in gold. Superhuman efforts had been, and were being, made to increase the gold in the Reichsbank. The gold had now reached about 106 millions, and, in his opinion, therefore, it was necessary for them to make up their minds that there would be no cessation of the war on account of the gold position in Germany, at all events,with- in twelve months, and it might be longer. He did not, say there might not be a cessation of hostilities for other reasons. The weakness, he thought, would first show-itself, if it had not already done so, in Austria-Hungary. Tlie groat confidence shown by depositors in their respective institutions was highly gratifying to bankers, and a debt of gratitude was due to the Press for intelligently advising the public to continue their confidence. -
A dividend of 18 per cent. for the year, less income-tax, was declared.

div.head: GREATER MENACE THAN INVASION.
div.p: GREATER MENACE THAN INVASION.
The Rev. J. E. Rattenbury at Padgate.

The Rev. J. E. Rattenbury paid a welcome return visit to the Padgate Wesleyan Church ; on Thursday and met with a hearty reception from the members of the congregation, who turned up in good numbers to a devotional ser- vice conducted by, the reverend gentleman in the afternoon and a lecture he gave in the even- ing. In his sermon Mr. Rattenbury dealt with the subject of the futility of all culture and all progress in the finer arts unless it was accom- panied by the spirit of Christ and a love of sacrifice and godliness. His lecture was on the subject of " The War and the Churches," and, in the course of it, he pointed out that many complex questions, social and otherwise, would arise as an aftermath of the present crisis, not the least of them being that of the drink traffic, and, concerning all 'ef which, it would be the Church's duty to step in more courageously than hitherto and grapple with them. As to the great issue that was being decided on the plains of Europe, he believed that this country was to-day engaged in a war that was certainly as Christian a war as ever was likely to be. "I daresay," said the speaker, "that we do not love the Germans as well as we used to do, but we shall love them again when we have beaten them." (Hear, hear.) • That was a great char- acteristic of the English people, as they saw exemplified in the case of the Boers. The speaker went on to describe the drink traffic in this country as a greater menace than the threatened German invasion; it had killed more men than' ever this war had, or would. They had, he said, made more trouble because a com- paratively few people were killed at Scarborough and the Hartlepools the other week, than they had over the hundreds of thousands who had been slain during the past few years, in this country alone, by alcohol. Other of the warring nations had felt that drink was the enemy as well as Germany, and had resolved to fight both foes simultaneously. The lecturer was accorded hearty thanks, on the proposition of Dr. Bennett, seconded. by Mr. Newton, and during the evening a collec- tion was made on behalf of the funds of the .Wesley Guild, which was responsible fbr bring- ing Mr. Rattenbury down to Padgate.

div.head: WAR CONTRASTS.
div.p: WAR CONTRASTS.
German Decadence in the Course of Forty Years.
BY C. E. PARKER.

Forty-four years ago this day (January 28th, 1871) Paris capitulated to the Germans, thus six months after the war began. It is a strikizg coincidence that the Franco-German War be- gan precisely on the same date as the present war. France declared war on Germany on July 14th, 1870, but it took Germany eighteen dayz; to mobilise her army, and the conflict actually began on August 3rd, the same date this i'ear as Germany declared war on• prance, and the day after—some say the same day—invaded Belgium. In 1870 Germany and France pro- mised ,England to respect the neutrality of Belgium; in other words, covenanted by signed engagement to respect the existing treaty. This was brought about by the action of England, who intimated that if either country violated this neutrality England would use force to de- fend Belgium against the transgressor.

div.head: Gladstone and Belgian Integrity.
div.p: Gladstone and Belgian Integrity.

John Bright was very uneasy lest this ulti- matum would drag England into war. By the re-affirmation of the treaty obligation Gladstone hoped to render improbable to the very last degree either of the nations laying hands upon Belgium, and wrote to Bright:— "But that the Belgians, whether they would .or not, should go 'plump' down the maw of 'another country to satisfy dynastic greed, is another matter. The accomplishment of such a crime as this implies, would come near to the extinction of public right in Europe." - At the time of the capitulation of Paris the number of dead, wounded, and missing during the war was estimated at 120,000, not including prisoners. This, I suppose, will represent about a tenth of the French and one-twentieth of the German casualties in the present war to date.

The cost of the first .war to France was esti- mated at £120,000 a day; now it is over £1,000,000. . One incident by way of contrast in connection with the capitulation of Paris is of interest. The Germans recognised that hunger would bring about surrender, and large supplies of provisions were sent forward from Germany in anticipa- tion of the need, sa much so that the military complained of the hlockage of the lines be- ' tween Germany and Paris by the food train. For several days after the capitulation the population of Paris, over 2,000,000, were fed by their German conquerors. This is very different from the canduct of the Germans to the Bel- gians, who are reduced to want by their Mis- deeds. After reading the newspapers and other .records of the period, I have come to the con- clusion that the way in which that war was conducted by the Germans was far more humane than in the present war. That there was stern severity there is no doubt, hut there was an absence of that useless brutality, which has characterised the Germans in this conflict, espe- cially in connection with their treatment of the Belgian people. War, Not Theatricals.

Another point of contrast is the difference in the German attitude to their opponents. In 1870 there was none of that organised orgy of hate which has characterised the present struggle, none of that surrender to the basest emotionalism and general lack of steady nerve. Then it was the French who talked at the top of their voice, and not, as now, the Germane. The Germans manifested a restrained power, a great purposeful strength. Now the French show these characteristics. Lack of these quali- ties has been evidenced in the military opera- tions. In 1870 the great German General von Moltke ever kept in view the military object, and silently but effectually concentrated his energies upon it. In the cbnflict of to-day, both in the eastern and western front, the mili- tary objects have been sacrificed to political aims. The theatrical design of getting to Calais through Flanders, and bombarding Scarborough and Yarmouth to terrorise the British are in- stances of German military ineptitude. In regard to the hysterical evidences of hate of which we daily read in extracts from the German Press, we may surely entertain the hope thlt the Press does not accurately repre- sent the feelings of the majority of the German people, and that in their papers we get the froth and scum of the thought of a section, and that underneath, and inarticulate, there is a great deal of sanity and good feeling which only need fitting conditions to find expression. It is interesting to see how Belgium heliavrd in the stirring times of 1870. Tier neutrality and freedom .from invasion being protected by the strong action of England, she was enabled to keep her country safe, and just as :Holland is now acting, Belgium then became a harbour of refuge to the non-combatants and a hospital for the wounded of both sides. The following extracts from Press notices at the time show this.

div.head: Germany Returns Evil for Good.
div.p: Germany Returns Evil for Good.

I have Culled the following from the files of the "Daily Telegraph" : " From her proximity to the seat of war, Bel- gium has nobly undertaken to receive and attend. to as many wounded as could be con- veyed from the battlefields round Sedan. Num- bers of these gallant sufferers have been accom- modated at Namur,, Charleroi, and other fron- tier towns; and, though much further removed

from the scene of action, Brussels, by means of the Luxemburg railway, has within the last week many wounded, chiefly French, the Germans having been conveyed to their cwn country by way of Liege. Several public buildings have been converted into hospitals, provided -with every possible attendance; and many private individuals have offered their houses for the same charitable purpose.

"For the moment the work of charity absorbs the whole of the energies of Belgium. Hospi- tals are organised everywhere in the towns and in the country, in public buildings and in the homes of citizens of every class. "I hear that the French soldiers, besides testifying their gratitude for the manner in which they are treated by the population, can- not refrain from expressing their surprise at, the beauty of the city and the wealth and pros- perity which its aspect betokens. In common with many of their compatriots of 7t much higher social , status, they imagined that there was no place except Paris for a civilised being to inhabit, and the fortune of war, which has made them partakers of the hospitality and kindness of the Belgian population, will thin; have a beneficial influence on the development of their intellect. The geographical ignorance of the French, even of the higher classes, is notorious: . . Confining myself, therefore, to Brussels, I can assert, without fear of con- tradiction, that the capital of free and happy Beleium is adding a noble page to her history, and that the conduct of her inhabitants is worthy of the example set them by their fathers in 1815, whose truly Christian conduct towards the wounded of Waterloo acquired for them a world-wide renown for humanity, imperishably recorded in the proclamations of Wellington and Blucher !"
