div.head: JOITINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOITINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
" What'il You Have?"

From what that gentleman said at the Liberal Club last week, Alderman Tinnion, although a total abstainer, would have been hail-fellow- -well-met in certain days that I wot of, wher printors were a notoriously thirsty class. I re- number a story of a newspaper staff, one dry raid-week in summer-when funds were low, marching in a body to their favourite pub ever the way, and obtaining a cheap drink by a trick. Said the spokesman, "George, we've had a little dispute and we want you to settle it. Ought one to say, GEintlemen, what will you have to drink?' or Gentlemen, what will you have to take?' " "That's easily settled," promptly re- sponded the, unsuspecting George; "Gentle- men, what will you have to drink?' " Upon which the company chorused their thanks, and each proceeded to "give it aflame." The land- lord said it was all right for once, but they "musn't come it again." Our Debt of Honour.

Mr. Charles E. Parker suggests that Warring- ton should be prepared to. hospitably entertain more than the present forty-two homeless Bel- gians. I think so, too. Some of the districts in which I have lived are certainly doing much better. I know of one place of only 8,000 in- habitants that is already providing for more of these poor people than Warrington has yet in- vited, and the limit has not yet been reached. I am acquainted with several yell-to-do citizens who have not only placed furnished housts at the disposal of families of these. distressed for- eigners, but guaranteed their support for twelve months. Moreover, the public generally are doing their utmost to alleviate their sad lot. They are regularly invited to entertainments and social functions, taken for motor runs, and the men are made honorary members of the local clubs; in short, whatever occurs to their hosts as calculated to help them temporarily to forget their miserable condition is at once acted upon. Those in Warrington have been made to feel at home, and are as comfortable as possible; but one cannot but agree with Mr. Parker when he urges that the number ought te greatly multiplied.- Our City Fathers. - -

The local par respecting Town Council photo- graphs somehow reminded me of the following; A little boy was reading a newspaper. Look- ing up he said: "Town councillors are called city fathers, aren't they, pa?" "Yes, my son." "Well, what's the difference between them and other fathers?"

"There is very little difference. As a general thing the sons run in debt and their fathers have to pay, but the city fathers contract debts and their sons, and even their grandsons, have' to pay. That's the difference, my son !"

Antiseptic Surgery. ' Under the sub-head "Science and Disease" in last week's "Chat and Gossip" by V Marjorie," there was an allusion to the Lister treatment knnwn as above. I recall a statement by an eminent surgeon that Lord Lister succeeded in applying scientific and practical surgery to the benefit of mankind and to the sparing of humali life and suffering more than any other person who has ever lived. In a congratulatory letter once addressed to the then octogenarian in his retirement, the Royal College of Surgeons de- clared:—

• - "As time passes, the blessings which have followed your life's work have been innumer- able, and the knowledge that ihey become each „year more and more manifest must, we feel assured, be a source of extreme consolation to you in your distinguished and hrourable re- tirement."

The contributor to "Woman's World" does well to remind her readers of these things. But for Lord Lister, hosts or wounded soldiers now happily in various stages of convalescence would now have been in their graves. Nonsense Wore*.

Mr. Hy. Brierley's lecture on ecclesiastical words started for me a train of thought which led to the point indicated in my headline, and I turned up a compilation by a well-known authority recalling such made-up nameis as Bongtree and Borogrove, and adjectives like runcible and vorpal, for which the reader will search his dictionary in vain. Then there are monxome, beamish, Attery Squash, Pobble, Jumbly, Lilliput, Brobdingnag, Laputa, Blefuscu, S'kyresh, Bolgoram, Flimnap, Nardac, glurr, glumgruff, glumigrim, Blundeeral, splack- nnck, Glumdalclitch, Lorbrulgrud, Struldbrugs, Glubbdubdribb, Truldragdubh, &c., • mostly ,of Dean Swift's inventing,. lam further reminded (and with this the compositor if not the reader will be glad to know I conclude the reference) that there was .the ceremonial phrase employed in approaching the Luggnaggian throne: "Ickpling gloffthrob squutserumm blhiop •talaslmalt zwin knodbalkuffh -slhiophad gurd- lubh asht "—which meant: "May your Celes- tial Majesty outlive the sun eleven moons and a half."

Thackeray and Dickens. - Mr. DEtvid P. Boyd's commendation of Dickens and two or three other novelists at the Adult School gathering reported in last week's "Ex- aminer," reminded me how I used to contend for the immortal Charles against a late colleague on the staff of a Yorkshire paper, who swore by Thackeray. He would take lofty ground, and talk of the correct style, the pure English, and the highly finished method of his idol, contrast- ing these with what he termed the crudities, ex- travagances, and exaggerations of mine. Then would I, in the like superior manner, denounce Thackeray as a shallow critic and prate of his tiresome commonplace moralising. Of course, it was all futile and foolish 'enough, and for my part I would fain make all possible atonement by urging my young readers to give a fair pro- portion of their leisure to the delightful crea- tions of both masters in question.

Boys, Don't Smoke. - I am going to take the liberty to devote my- remaining space to a homily on a text provided by "Uncle Ned" in the " Children's Corner" a week ago. div.head: GOWYS GLORY.
div.p: THE GOWYS GLORY.

Sir,—Your Angling Notes of last week con- tain a.. somewhat curious document. I refer to Mr. Knight's annual report of the Warrington Anglers' Association. Why this report should contairi any reference to the Gowy, with which the Warrington Anglers' Association has noth- ing whatever to do, I am utterly at a loss to understand, but when that reference is quite contrary to fact, and is calculated to be very detrimental to the interests of another society, I am constrained ,to protest, and to protest as strongly as I know how, 'on behalf of that society.

div.head: INCREASED DRUNKENNESS IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: INCREASED DRUNKENNESS IN WARRINGTON.

Sir,—The awfully black annual report of the Chief Constable of Warrington adds another sad chapter to the history of this otherwise good old town. After all the efforts of the true social reformers, the blighting influence of the trade in intoxicating drink: has during the year 1914 claimed an addition of 61 victims more than in the previous year. Thus the abnormal total of persons proceeded against for drunkenness reached the alarming number of 615. The report -states that during the last five months of the year (war period) there was a decrease of 66 in the number of persons pro- ceeded against, as compared with the same period of 1913; so that we must conclude that during the first seven mouths from January to August of 1914 drunkenness was far above nor- mal amongst the civil population, and that apart from the war the authorities would have been justified in putting into operation the special Act- for curtailing the hours of Sale, to 'save the inhabitants from the ravages of the trade.

But, alas! when approached by the Rector (Canon Willis) and other ministers of religion in the town with a petition praying that the Act should be applied in ytirarrington, they were simply told by the offioials that there was no necessity to take any action. In the light of the Chief Constable's annual report the passive attitude assumed by those in authority seems- to be 'absolutely indefensible. When are the ratepayers going to assert themselves and demand that this growing evil of intemperance in our good old town shall be stayed?
SOBRIETY.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST —continued.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST —continued.

country at a former period. Nearne, the diarist, has this in his reference to the great plague : - "Even children were-obliged to smoak. And I remember that I heard 'formerly Tom Rogers, who was yeoman beadle, say that when he was a schoolboy at Eton that year when. the Plague raged all the boys in the school were obliged to smoakin the school every morning, and that he was never whipped so much in his life as he was one morning for not smoaking." Medical Testimony. In these enlightened days, however, eminent men in all ranks of life agree in warning boys against the habit in question, and foremost among these are doctors whose scientific attain- ments give very considerable weight to their opinions. Sir William Broadbent confessed on at least-one occasion that he-would like to make smoking before -the age of '2l a 'punishable offence, his conviction being that the worst mis- chief worked by the tobacco habit is done prior to that age. He declares that tobacco affects the heart and nerves and digestion most seri- ously in the young, and that early smoking tends to establish habits of self-indulgence, which, with the enervating influence of tobacco. are fatal to efficiency and strength of character. Sir Benjamin Ward Richardson goes further, showing the dire effects on succeeding genera- tions, and "making no bones about ft." I know of another doctor who examined thirty boy-smokers, between the ages of nine and fif- teen. In twenty-two he round serious disorders, and a more or less marked taste, generated by tobacco, for drink. • Evil Effects.

According to officials of anti-tobacco organisa- tions, tobacco is the admitted cause of upwards of eighty diseases, including blindness and can- cer of the lower lip and tongue, and is credited with killing 20,000 in our land every year. They tell us, moreover—and support their contention by formidable facts and figures—that boys who. smoke seem to have their moral sensibilities blunted, so that they are led easily into other vices. Prison statistics show that an enormous percentage of all male convicts started their downward career by smoking and drinking. In one prison, of 600 prisoners, confined for crimes committed under the influence of drink, 500 tes- tified that they began their intemperance by smoking. " kia.tele Ned" is evidently desirous of assisting in the creation of an anti-smoking sentiment among the boys themselves; and as- suredly there is more to be hoped from that than from legislative enactments which those in authority find it difficult to enforce. Do any oi our Boy Scouts smoke? If they do, they are acting directly contrary to the stipulations of their revered chief.

div.head: COAL SHORTAGE.
div.p: COAL SHORTAGE.
A long agenda was got through at the fort- nightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, held at the Workhouse on Wednes- day morning, Mr. A. J. Jolley presiding.

div.head: SCARCITY OF COAL.
div.p: THE SCARCITY OF COAL.

Reference was made in the minutes of the House Visiting Committee to the scarcity of coil, and a recommendation of the committee was adopted that in view of the shortage and increased difficulties in obtaining coal, the com- mittee be recommended to advertise for tenders for 100 tons immediately. A letter bearing on the subject was read from the coal contractors; the Pearson and Knowles

The position is serious in the -extreme, and it will be quite impossible for 'us to produce the quantities-of coal which we have contracted for, in which case we shall have to limit our • deliveries to all contractors proportionately. You may be assured that we shall do all we possibly can for you and all our contractors, but we have no other option than to give you this notice."

div.head: GUARDIANS' APPRECIATION OF THE LATE MR. LAWRANCE.
div.p: GUARDIANS' APPRECIATION OF THE LATE MR. LAWRANCE.

The proceedings of the Padgate Homes and Schools Committee, which. were approved, con- tained the following vote of condolence: "The committee place on record their sincere sorrow at .the loss sustained by the death of -Mr. C. E. Lawrance, superintendent of the homes, whose unfailing kindness and courtesy to the children and general organising ability have been, highly appreciated by the Guardians during his period of service with the Union." The Chairman said he would like to associate himself with the resolution. Personally, he thought the institution had suffered a great loss by the untimely removal of one of -their ser- vants. He was sure that all their sympathies would go out to the family. _ _ _ _

Miss Broadbent s'aid they had suffered a very great loss indeed, and she was more sorry than she could say. Mr. Lawrance's whole heart was in the school; in fact, he never spoke of any- thing else except the' children.

div.head: VACANT SCHOOLMASTERSHIP.
div.p: THE VACANT SCHOOLMASTERSHIP.

The Chairman said the question of appointing a successor would be considered at a special meeting of the Padgate Homes and School Com- mittee, to be held a month hence. He -added that it was not a matter of great urgency. Mr. Lee remarked that he .thought it was of great urgency, as there had not been any school- master or assistant for some. time..
The Chairman asked if the speaker made any alternative suggestion. Mr. Lee: I think we ought to consider it at the next meeting. _ _ _ _ _

Mr. Mather said help could not be got. They had been waitibg a month, he believed, for temporary help, and it had not been forthcom- ing. He did not know whether it was a pressing matter. They had two certificated teachers and uncertificated teachers, and there were only about 140 children in the schools. Ile asked Mr. Lee not to press his amendment. It would be as well to let things 'calm down, and in a month's time they would be better able to judge. Mr. Lee: I do not mind at all!

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER AND CHAPLAIN.
div.p: MEDICAL OFFICER AND CHAPLAIN.
The salary of Dr. W. J. Peacocke, medical officer of the Padgate Cottage Homes and Schools, was increased from £3O per annum to £5O.

Mr. Brooks proposed that the Chairman and Vice-Chairman of the Board, together with the Clerk, be appointed as delegates to attend the annual meeting of the Central Poor Law Con- ference, to be held in: London on the 9th and 10th February, 1915. The resolution was seconded.

Miss Broadbent, remarking that the lady members had no chance in these things, although they took a great interest in the work of the Board, moved, .as an amendment, that Mrs. Hall be added to the number of delegates. div.p: SHOULD BE IN ASYLUMS.

The Lunacy Commissioners wrote to the effect that they considered many of the cases which were now receiving workhouse treatment were really,cases that should be treated-in the County Asylums, and thatAin their opinion, provision should be made with the County Asylum for the reception of such cases. div.p: GUARDIANS AND MILITARY PATIENTS

div.head: Dies From Injuries Received On His
div.p: Dies From Injuries Received On His
Round.

An inquiry was held by Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner for South-West Lancashire, at the Warrington. Coroner's Court on Monday, into the circumstances concerning the death of Alfred Whitley, 52 years,. of 14, Chapel-lane, Stockton Heath, who died at the Warrington Infirmary on January gist..* Ada Whitley, who stated that she was the wife of the deceased, said that about 7.40 a.m. on Tuesday, January sth, her husband left the house to follow his usual employment, that of a licensed hawker. He was then in his usual good health and spirits. At about 8.45 a.m. she learnt that her .husband had met with an acci- dent and had been taken to the Wafrington Infirmary. In company with the deceased was his brother Joshua, and the witness at once went to the Infirmary and saw her husband there.
Harness Broke, and He was Thrown over Pony's Head.

He was then quite conscious, and told her that he was going down the hill at tumb Brook with his pony and cart, when the back band of the harness broke, and the shafts went forward and with a sudden jerk threw him over the pony's head on to the road. His feet then became en- tangled with the reins, which dragged him about 50 yards along the road. From the time of his admittance to the Infirmary to the time of his death, the witness added, she had frequently visited her husband.
In reply to the Deputy Coroner, the witness said the deceased had had the pony two years last October.
Tried to Stop the Pony.

Charles Rylands, gardener,' 2O Oreliard7street, Stockton Heath, spoke to proceeding along the sanie road as the deceased with his pony and cart, when he heard someone shouting "Whoa." He turned round and saw the deceased alight on the road. Witness immediately ran to Whit- ley's assistance. He sent for a taxi cab and at once conveyed the injured man to the Warring- ton Infirmary,, where Whitley was detained as an in-patient. ' Witness was of, the opinion that the deceased must have been trying to stop the pony, as he held the reins in his hands. Answering the Deputy Coroner, witness said the deceased was lying in the roadside when he came up and the pony, which 'had- srepped, was a short distance away.

div.head: Death Due to Shock.
div.p: Death Due to Shock.

J. B. Anderson, police clerk in the Warring- ton borough force, deposed to making inquiries at the Infirmary into the deceased's death, and stated that he was informed by the doctor that death took place on January 21, and was due to shock following the accident. There was a wound, but that in itself had not caused death. The doctor also informed witness that the de- ceased's heart and lungs were in a very weak condition. •
The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

div.head: PADGATE CHURCH EXPENSES.
div.p: PADGATE CHURCH EXPENSES.
Guardians' Grant on Behalf of the Children.

The question of making a grant to the Pad- gate Parish Church towards the cost of heat- ing, lighting, &c., came before the Warrington Guardians at their meeting on Wednesday, when it was decided to contribute —1;10 per annum.

div.head: £lO SUBSCRIPTION SUGGESTED.
div.p: A £lO SUBSCRIPTION SUGGESTED.

Mr. Mather moved: "That a grant of a sum not exceeding £lO per arinum be made to the churchwardens of the Parish Church, Padgate, as a contribution towards the expenses of heat- ing, cleaning and lighting-the- said church, used by the children ot the Cottage Homes." In doing so, he said that this matter had been much discussed in other ways before. The situ- ation was that the church had to be cleaned, lighted and heated, and the expense had to come from somewhere, and he did not think the Board wanted the congregation of the church at Pad- gate to pay all the expenses without subscribing something towards them. Mr. Lee seconded.

Mr. Dale .asked whether the children referred to in the• resolution were the same as the .Rev. A. Al. Mitchell alluded to in a resolution -at the last meeting. Mr. Lee: Yes. They are all Church of Eng- land.children. Mr. Dale: Are there.no Free Church children in the institution? .
The Chairman: It is hardly probable tlial there are. It all depends how they are regis- tered.
NOT A BUSINESS PROPOSITION.

The Rev. A. M. Mitchell declared that he was sorry that this particular resolution had been put forward in its present form. Looking at it from a business point of view, he did not think the resolution was in order. He thought it made statements which would not bear inspection. He would like to know where the lighting came in. So far as his knowledr went, the children attended. service on Sunday mornings. They were not present on Sunday evenings. If the officers attended in the evening he concluded that they made their own contributions to the offertory. Therefore, he did not think there was any ground for asking for a grant on the score of lighting. As regards heating, he supposed that Mr. Mather would find that if these chil- dren did not attend that the church would 'still be heated. And as regards pleading for a grant for cleaning, surely the church Would have to be cleaned from end to end whether the children were there or not, and he did not think it would make any difference to the wages of the women who cleaned the House of God. Looking at the matter from this business point of view, he did not think Mr. Mather's resolution. was a very sound one. He thought that every person ought to contribute towards the support of the church. The question of equity on the floor of God's House and the question of financial aid was a vital one, and if they were going to deal with it in this way they would be doing it in the wrong way. He was sorry that he could not support Mr. Mather's resolution, but he would not oppose it.

div.head: MORALLY, IF NOT LEGALLY, BOUND.
div.p: MORALLY, IF NOT LEGALLY, BOUND.

Mr. Dennett also said he could not support the resolution, but would not oppose it. • Replying, Mr. Mather said that with regard to the lighting, the children went in the early morning, when the lights were lit, lie could not see for one moment why anybody should object to giving something towards the expense of cleaning, lighting and heating the church. The Union was morally bound to do so, if not legally hound. The Chairman mentioned that the matter would' be subject .to the approval of the Local, Government Board:
The original motion was carried by 9 rotes to 2, and two members did not vote.

div.head: LYMM SOLDIERS' 11101,111).1Y.
div.p: LYMM SOLDIERS' 11101,111).1Y.
Departures anti Arrivals—A Whirl of
Excitement.

At the Lymm Parish Church on Sunday morning, .the twenty-five local Territorials 'who were that day concluding their five days' leave, paraded. The service created a profound im- pression upon all who attended, the Rector (the Rev. G. B. Thurston) occupying the pulpit. At the conclusion Mr.' Thurston. spoke very appro- priately to the men, and wished them God- speed and good luck in their. Mission. The hearers were much affected.

div.head: Au Revoir—and a Welcome!
div.p: Au Revoir—and a Welcome!

In charge of Sergeant Harold Clare, this first batch departed at half-past eight on Sunday evening, when they had a splendid send-off from the station. A very large crowd gathered to bid them "good-bye," and as the train steamed away bound for C (in the East) the cheer- ing was loud and prolonged. , The following day another batch of a dozen arrived for their five days' leave, since when others have also come—amongst them Captain Hartley, to see whom everybody has been very pleased, as his absence whilst engaged in the work of .the Army has been a somewhat lengthy one. The "Tommies" who do not return to their station on Saturday will do so the day after. Many of these men were unable—owing to stress of duty in another part of the country —to pay a visit to Lymm at Christmas or the New Year, so that it can readily be guessed how they have looked forward to, and are en- joying, the visit now. This weeZ "The Examiner" representative has interviewed competent -military authorities with regard to the work of the Lymm soldiers, and he, has been assured that the -Lymm and Frodsham men—who now belong to the same Brigade, under a new scheme of battalion organ- isation—are certainly quite equal to any oth4rs to be found in the battalion, if not in th 6 brigade! They surpass them especially in mili- tary marching and entrenchment. The discip- line is excellent, and the spirits of the men leave nothing to be desired; they are "on the best of terms" with their officers.
Whither Away?

To a question as to where the Lymm " Tommies'.! are going after their return to the East, the only reply our representative could obtain was: " The men don't mind where they go, and it is always the unexpected that hap- pens. They may go to France. But remember the rumour in November which said they were going to India—they never went! Therefore do not place too much importance on these rumours."

div.head: COUNCIL SERVANTS ON ACTIVE SERVICE.
div.p: COUNCIL SERVANTS ON ACTIVE SERVICE.
New Employes May Not Get Half- Wages Allowed.

The Lymm Council, at a meeting held on August 17th last year, passed the following resolution: "That all employes of the Council called out, Or who may volunteer for service during the war, be paid half wages during their absence, and that their positions ,be kept open for them on their return."

At Monday evening's meeting of the Counail the principal interest centred in an amend- ment to this resolution, which stood on the agenda to the 'name of Councillor Cowper, namely, "That the resolution passed on the 17th of August last_ with regard to paying half wages to employes absent during the period of war only refeis to employes of the Council at the date of the passing of the resolution, and not to employes engaged since.',' The Purpose of the Resolution.

•In moving this •amendment, Councillor Cowper said he considered it only fair that the Council should make this stipulation. They might have a number of men who, after coming in and working for theii. only a short time— perhaps only a week—might go and join the forces and expect the Council to pay !them half wages. As district councillors they should pay regard to all these payments and look after the interests of the ratepayers. It was not that they did not think highly of these men—all the councillors were anxious to do what they could for the country—but he thought it only fair that the resolution should not refer to fresh employes. • " Lymm Has Done So Well."

Councillor -Gotobed said that, as the mover of the original resohition, he seconded this one. Ile thought' they could safely pass it, because Lymm had done so well that it was unlikely that the Council would have occasion. to engage any of the classe men to which Mr. Cowper re- ferred. The original resolution had clearly been passed for the purpose of providing for those of their own employes who had left their work for the time being to serve their country ; and not for those Who came in for a week; Sub- sequently. The Clerk <Mr. W. Mullard) pointed out that

the word " permanent " might be put in the resolution before the word "employes," and the phrase "at the date of the passing of the resolu- tion" omitted, as the Surveyor had suggested. If not, would a man who had entered • the Council's employment two or three weeks before August 17th be entitled to half-pay?
Should Not Support Temporary Hands.

The marriage of Mr. Arthur John Warburton, of Booths Bank Farm, Rostherne, to Miss Alice Eva Winstanley, fourth daughter of Mr. John Winstanley, of Ryecroft, Lymm, was solemnised at the Wesleyan Church on Wednesday. Miss Winstanley is well known in Lymm, and has been an active worker in connection with several local societies, &c., especially the Sunday School, where for a little time past she has had charge of the primary class. She takes with her the good wishes of many friends in this district ad she will be much missed in many directions.

The Preston-o'-th)-Hill Housing Committee repot, which was read, stated that a letter from the Local Government Board was received, intimating they had had under consideration the report of their inspector, after his recent visit to the parish for tha purpose of investigat- ing the housing conditions, and suggested that the District Council should provide three bedded roomed houses under Part 111. of the Housing of the Working Classes Act. 1880- It waS 'resolved, that - (1)- the -Clerk write to the Manchester Ship Canal Company calling atten- tion to the requirements of the Local Govern- ment Board, and suggesting that if they could see their way to enlarge the cottagee belonging to them near the Canal Bridge so as to relieve the overcrowding, probably the expenses of pro- viding further accommodation out of tike rates would be avoided; (2) that the Assistant Inspec; tor of Nuisances prepare a census of the parish, showing the number of houses and the number, relationship and age of the occupants of such houses. Mr. Spencer made a statement to the effect that 20 houses had been demolished and 24 had been erected since 1000. The Manchester Ship Canal Company had had alterations made to four houses near the Canal Bridge by the addi- tion of another bedroom to each house.

Mr. Woodwdrd said the present congestion, so far as the committee were able to discover, arose mainly, if not wholly with the property belong- ing to the Manchester Ship Canal Company. He pointed out that it was a Serious matter to ask a parish council like Preston-o'-th'-Hill to under- take the erection of workmen's dwellings, and they thought it would be better to appeal to the Canal Company to improve their property, which could be done at a reasonable cost. That appeared to be the best way of meeting the deadlock at the moment. If the" Canal 'Com- pany refused to do it, they would have to see what other steps could be devised. Mr. Spruce, seconding the - adoption of the report, .said the Canal Company had already enlarged some houses. , If four of te houses were' now enlarged it would relieve the situa- tion.
The report was adopted. A DANGEROUS OBSTRUCTION.

Warrington journeyed to Weaste on., Satur- day and beat Salford's reserves by eleven points te nil, though they had by no means- such an easy task on hand as the score might lead one to conclude, for the homesters were triers all the way through and neither gave nor asked quarter. Still, Warrington won, and after all that is the great thing from the point of view of local loyalists. Had they been on the top of their form it is possible they might have made an even bigger margin of it, but, as it was, their Play frequently erred on the side of scrappiness, and at least three glorious openings we wasted for the want of a little combination. They started Well enough, 'tis true, but they seemed to grow easily a-wearied, and before half-time as signalled their play had become .marked by a looseness that, against better opponents, might have cost them dear. The Salford men, opposed to superior weight, struggled gamely to the end, and had their skill been in any way commen- surate with their push and energy, it is pos- sible that the .score-board 'might have had a different tale to tell. The reason why War- rington came to he opposed to a team of players who usually are to be found in the ranks of Salford "A" will be fresh in the Minds of all followers of Northern Union football. They will recall that on a recent memorable Satur- day, when down to engage the Broughton Ran- gers, the Salford men, with one exception, re- fused to play, claiming that the ground was too frost-bound, despite the fact that the referee held otherwise. For this breach of rule twelve of the thirteen men concerned were placed on the suspended list until the end of. January.

Brookes scored the third and last try for Warrington shortly before the interval, crossing the line after a swinging run, during which he adroitly eluded several outstretched pairs of hands, itch- ing to Collar him. Jolley. missed .with the kick, the somewhat slippery state of the turf being a contributory cause to this, his second failure or the afternoon: The second half of the game was scoreless, although both sides tried hard to put on points, the Salford men working par- ticularly hard to open their account, though their efforts availed them nothing, and when the final whistle sounded they had made no tangible reply to the goal and three tries put up against them by the lads from Wilderspool.

div.head: SALFORD'S JUNIORS STRUGGLE GAMELY.
div.p: SALFORD'S JUNIORS STRUGGLE GAMELY.

The Warrington forwards started Saturday's game in businesslike fashion, and fora time it looked as if the game was going to be something in the nature of a walk-over ,for them. But it did not take the Salford men long to find their legs, so to speak, and by the end of the first half they were giving pretty well as good as they received, whilst in the second moiety they stoutly held their own, withstanding with pluck and success the many fierce onslaughts made upon them. However, before they had got the measure of their opponents the mischief—look- ing at it from their point of view—had been done, and the eleven points had been put up against them. They tried hard to reduce the balance, once they got warmed to their work, but. the Warrington defence proved as sotind- as a bank, and though they *orkedt all they knew- they were kept at a safe distance. Taken by and large, the game was not an uninteresting one, and Salford, under the peculiar circum- stances which compelled them to be represented by a reserve teqm, did quite as well, if not better' than most of the three thousand people on the ground anticipated. As we have said, the struggle was a determined ,one on the part of the homesters, and Warrington had no soft thing on hand.

div.p: WARRINGTON'S ALL-ROUND SUPE;;;ORITY.

Of course, nothing like the kudos attached to Saturday's win that would have belonged to it had it been scored over the team which, until the present pass was brought about, used to do duty for Salford—a team which had been spoken of as many-talented, and was said to have come along considerably since Warring- ton la'st had the pleasure of taking a rise out of them at Wilderspool. Still there was this satis- faction about Saturday's victory: that it broke a nine-year-old succession of defeats at Weaste. And, therefore, jubilation is justifiable. The Warringtonians showed superiority in every de- partment. They. worked the scrums 4bettier

than did their opponents, and their forwards were quicker and more resourceful, though the Salford. men made up in great measure for their lack in trickiness and speed by their deter- mination and pluck. However often .they were repulsed they came again, and they rarely missed taking even the remotest chances. • But want of 'cohesion doomed all thei efforts to failure; their game was purely of the opportunist order; Jolley, apart from his two faulty kicks at goal, played a sound game and experienced comparatively little difficulty in disposing of the opposition rushes. Harrison, too, was a hard worker for Salford, but he was kept a great deal buskr than Jolley, and amid his mul- tifarious duties might be pardoned for the one or two. slips he made.
FORWARDS' WANT OF COMBINATION.

Bradshaw and Tranter were the pick of the Warrington three-quarters, putting in much hard work, and Baker, too, was a useful man ou the three-quarter line. Young and Daiu- teth played strenuously, especially in the .first half, when they. proved thorns in the side to the homesters. Cox was the life and soul of the '.Warrington forward line, though the whole of the sextet did pretty well, but for the fact that they were, individually, somewhat too prone to forget that after all they were cogs on a wheel, and not the wheel of itself. • Occasionally the Sal- ford men delighted the crowd with individual efforts, 'upon -which they seemed to- rely' rather than upon good,- sound, concerted action; indeed; there • was hardly a suggestion of combination about their • work. Their forwards never re- laxed their efforts, abortive though they were, and they undoubtedly finished up the fresher of the two packs. The referee did not seem to have perfect control of the game at times, -and more than once a section of the crowd found, or fan- cied they found, occasion to signify their opinion lin the usual manner.

STOCKTON HEATH v. CADISHEAD WESLEVANS.

The above met on the West-avenue ground, before a fair number of Spectators. Both clubs were well represented, and Mr. H. Smith, of Latchford, had charge of the game. The home captain won the toss and Alf. Tay- lor set the ball rolling for the visitors. Fol- lowing the initial exchanges, the home forwards broke away. and Ellams was called upon to save his charge. From his, clearance the home for- wards quickly returned to the attack, when Pearce tested Ellams with a good shot, Harri- son clearing, the visitors' forwards gained pos- session and raced to the opposite end, where Stokes tried Hooper with a shot, bat found him equal to the occasion. Then followed some gooct play in mid-field, where the "Heathens" half- backs showed rare ,judgment in tackling. An injury to Vernon, their centre-forward, upset. the "Heathens" display, until he resumed. The visitors, who began to show an improvement in their game, got near the home goal; and Lowes opened the, score with a capital shot at 25 yards' range. Stung by this reverse, the "Heathens" made a determined raid on their opponents' goal, and, from Lloyd's centre, Smith equalised. Both teams, having now got warm to their work, played in ding-dong fashion, the ball travelling very quickly from end to end. Off- side against Smith, of the "Heathens," was followed by a. free-kick. to the visitors, from which Lowes gained the lead for his side. At half-time the scores were :—Cadishead, 2 goals; Stockton. Heath, 1 goal. On the resumption the game continued to be very fast and °Ailing. After ten minutes' play Lowes again scored for the visitors, -thus completing- the "hat trick." Shortly after the centre-kick, Lloyd received a good pass on the home right, and, racing away, beat the backs and scored a capital goal. The players now began to show signs of excitement and several of them had to be penalised by the-referee. A free-kick Was entrusted to Lloyd; ,aid he was. successful in making the scores equal: For a while the game was stubbornly contested, but towards the close the visitors, 'being well served by their height and .superior finish, got the better of the. home defence, and Lowes scored his fourth goal. Directly' afterwards Aaron Taylor, by scoring a fifth, goal, put the issue beyond doubt, and, at the call of time, the visitor's were deserving winners by 5 goals to 3.

On Saturday, on the Horse and 7ockey ground, the game between Longford and Orford White Star was contested .under very agreeable conditions, and before .a fairly good Crowd. The players, entered into the contest in vigorous fashion, and \in a good sportsmanlike manner. In such a match, where ,rivalry is very keen between the clubs, shady play was conspicuoul by its absence, and the game was -very muchi enjoyed by the spectators., The result, three goals to two in favour of. the White Star, was a very good reflex of the play, and the visitors, on their display, were entitled to the full points they gained. Throughout the game the visitors showed a better finish to their movements', and did not miss many opportunities of tesling the opposing goalkeeper. What the home team lacked in, finish they nearly made up for in dash, but it was in their final efforts where their weakness was most notable,, for they had several fine opportunities to get on. equal terms if. their forwards had shot better. Late in. the second half a splendid effort by Stevens just glanced over the cross-bar, when an -equaliser appeared certain. Sturgess, in the home- goal, made many smart saves and kept his side from b. heavier defeat. Both backs played a faiey good game. Smart, at centre-half, played a hard game throughout, and Stevens, at times, was seen to Advantage, but has often playA The forwards, as a whole, did not core-thine suffi- ciently well to get the best results of thc:ir efforts. For the visitors, Miller, when called upon, did well, but be had not as much to do as his vis-a-vis. Pilling was the better of the backs. The half-back division is t'.e) strongest part of the White Star team; and Caldwell played a cool and resourceful game, closely fol- lowed by Denny. Gifford was not at his best, owing to a recent accident from which he has not yet fully recovered. OY the fot wards the centre-forward and left-wing were the most dangerous, and the right might have done better had they had more opportunities given to them.

Elmwood Congregationalists received a visit from St. BarnabaS',.this being the first occasion on which the clubs had met in the League con- test. The home team was strengthened by the inclusion of Finch and Ashton, and a trial was given to Derbyshire, of the second team; whilst the visitors had'their full- team out. The first half was mostly in, favour of the visitors, and they managed to ,score four times, whilst the home team replied once:Derbyshire, in falling back to assist the defence, unfortunately scored for the visitors, but directly after he made amends by putting 01.1• through at the opposite end, thus having the. distinction of scoring for both sides in the same half. In the second portion the display of the Cemgregationplists was very much better, and the visitors were not able to increhse their lead, whilst Smith reduced the arrears against the home club.

Newton Congregationalists paid their first visit to the Fairfield United ground, and were not able to put a full team in the field, Law- rence and Beresfor& being notable absentees, whilst the home team: also were not at their usual strength. The game- was well conte#ed, and. the visitors for the greater portion' of the game fairly held their own, as it was only in the closing stages that the United asserted themselves and scored four goals very quickly, the result being five -against One in favour of the United. Clayton and Glover, the secre- taries of each club, had to don -the ,jerseys.

On the Vitriol-road. ground, the Earlestown Y.M.C.A. and the Warrington Central teams ! met for the first time. The visitors had their usual eleven out; but the home, team were not at their best, Riley being absent. The visitors proved •too good for the Y.M:C.A. and scored twice before the interval.' In "the _second portion the home team re=arranged their team and were seen to much better advantage, but they were unable to pierce the Central's defence, -Ashcroft and Glover defending stoutly. Gilbert, at centre-half, did well, .Farrell, Holmes and S. Mason being the best forwards. Martin, in goal, made many fine saves, and Lee -was the best in the back division. The half-back line was not as good as usual. Barlow and Hughes were the most prominent .in the forward line. Had the latter got better support from his colleagues, the result quite possibly may have favoured the home team. The visitors are to be congratulated on their display and victory on their opponents' ground. •1-

At the Paddington ground the Earlestown Mission team were the visitors, and the game was keenly contested for the greater portion of the time. The visitors led by the only goal at the interval.. In ,the second half the home team lost the services. of Knight, their goalkeeper, who, up to this time, had been of great service to his side, making several daring saves, and it was when attempting another that he came in contact with one of the opposing forwards .and had to retire. At the close of the game he was taken to the Warrington Infirmary and on ex- amination was found to have sustained, a broken nose. Upon making later inquiries, we are pleased .to .state that Knight is progressing very favourably. At the time of the accident there was only a few minutes left to play, and it was decided to continue the game. However, .before the finish the visitors added- another goal and won by two goals to. none.,

In the Altrincham and District-Amateur Cup- tie, Stockton Heath had .Cadishead Wesleyans as visitors, and as these two teams had met on two previous occasions in League contest and played drawn games, the cup-tie was looked upon as the rubber game. As the "Heathens" had choice of ground, they theld an advantage over their opponents. Ile Visitors were strongly represented, whilst the home team were minus the, services of .Bates, ,owing to in- jury. The game was very keenly contested throughout, and 'once the Visitors settled to their work they showed good understanding with .each other; whilst one Or' two of ,the home players appeared to have a roving commission, ,and, owing to that alone, several good scoring chances were lost. The final score- was 5-3 in 'favour of the visitors, and onetheir display - they were value for that result. At the close of the game the home players acknowledged they were defeated by a better team than themselves.

Grappenhall, another of our local clubs, were playing in the same competition at Knutsfqrd- road, where Altrincham St. Margaret's were the visitors. The game was very keenly and strenuously contested, no score being Made by either side in the first half. Early in the second portion the "Saints" gained, the lead. Grappenhall :soon followed With the equaliser, and then the lead was taken by the home playerS. After the visitors had made the scores equal. again there was -a keen '‘truggle for the lead. which the visitors eventually 'succeeded in ohtaining, the result being 3-2 in their favour.

Referee J. Smith. be I It was soon evident that the game was to keenly contested, and a very fast pace was set. The first advance was made by the visitors, but the home backs cleared their lines, and. then a visit was made to the opposite end, Where the visitors' half-backs, as a line, were very pro- , ntinent, and play was' transferred to the home ' quarters, Sturgess clearing finely. The visiting forwards returned to the attack and Stubbq 'scored for the White Star with a good shot, After this. early .reverse the home team in- creased their 'efforts, and 'after .a few futile attempts to break through they were successful in defeating the visitors' backs, and Hands equalised. The game was now contested in, ding-dong fashion, and both ends were 'visited, the backs. on both' sides playing a confident game, but the visitors' superiority lay in their middle line.. On several occasions Sturgess brought off good saves, and as the visitors .gradually closed in on the home defence pan- kinSon put the White Star in front again. The home lot Made desperate efforts to get on level terms again, but Evans and Piling' stuck to their ground in .splendid style, and Miller was not often called upon. Finch on one occasion missed a fine chance of scoring by easing up to shoot instead of taking the first chance, and the ball was sent wide of the goal. The tame was again transferred to the home quarters, where Hankinson, Meachin and Sttibbi were altvaW dangerous and eager to snap up any openings that came to them ; and after a couple' of corner-kicks had been cleared by the home defence, Hankinson at length got posseSSion and scored the visitors' third goal: Half-time:— White Star, 3 goals; Longford, 1 goal. After several keen attacks by the United had been repulsed, Hands succeeded in heading the ball through the top corner of the goal, Miller being at the opposite end.. As the end was approaching the players on both sides began to show signs of tiring, as the game had been very strenuously contested, and at the call of time the result was :—Orford White Star, 3 goals; Longford, 2 goals.

div.p: FORESTERS. BURIAL SOCIETY.
Record Year Reported at Annual Meeting.
The annual meeting of members of the Ancient Order of Foresters (Warrington Dis- trict Burial Society) was held at the Roebuck Hottel, Bridge-street, on Tuesday evening, Mr. Alfred Tilling presiding.

div.head: SATISFACTORY REPORTS.
div.p: SATISFACTORY REPORTS.
The Auditors (Messrs. George Rotherham and James Walsh) and the Examiner (Mr. George Maybury) gave their reports, which showed the affairs of the society to be conducted in a satis- factory manner.

The Secretary (Mr. L. Davies) gave a very interesting report of the working of the society during 1914, and stated that, although the country was passing through a dark and un- eettled period, the year had been the best the society had experienced, both from the numerical and financial standpoints, since its establish- ment forty-three years ago.

div.head: THOSE IN AUTHORITY.
div.p: THOSE IN AUTHORITY.

The following officers were elected for the ensuing twelve months;—President, the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock); vice-president, Mr. George Rotherham; trustees, Messrs. Alfred Tilling, George Maybury and William Hipkiss; treasurer, Councillor John Chrimes; secretary, Mr. L. Davies; assistant secretary, Mr. J. Da vies.
Grants of three guineas each were made to the Warrington Infirmary and the Nursing Association.
THE RULES REVISED.

After the annual meeting & special meeting was held for the purpose of amending the rules of the society. The chair was taken by the newly-appointed President, and, in opening the meeting, his Worship impressed upon the members the reason for, and desirability of, keeping the rules and regulations up-to-date and on the best pos- sible business footing. That was the aim of the Committee of Management. He felt sure that the present success of the society was, tea great extent, due to the new tables which had been placed before the general public, and also to the fact that steps had been taken to make it known that the society was open to anyone to join, and was not confined to Foresters alone. The new rules, having been thoroughly dis- cussed, were passed.

How the /AM B. Percival Would Encourage Churchgoing.

The annual parochial tea party in connection with St. Peter's Church, which was held on Monday evening in the .7 ohn-street School, and at which there was a very good attendance, was followed by an excellent entertainment, over which Mr. T. S. Steel (Vicar's warden) pre- sided.

div.head: MISSIONARY WORK FOR ALL.
div.p: MISSIONARY WORK FOR ALL.

During the evening the Vicar (the Rev. B. Percival), in a short speech, moved a hearty vote of thanks to the tray-givers, workers and entertainers. This was unanimously carried. The Vicar also referred to the, " Come-to- Church " Campaign, which commenced on the 24th inst., and would end on the 31st inst. That, he said, was a campaign which he had inaugur- ated in St. Peter's parish when he first came to it 22 years ago, and which he had carried on ever since.

It was for that purpose he had employed an assistant curate and a Church Army captain, that every one in the parish might be visited, whatever his creed might be, and it would be the delight of his heart to see the people crowd- ing into the church on Sundays—morning, after- noon, and evening, He wanted them all to become interested in the work of the Church— to becom% missionaries. SATURDAY SUGGESTED AS EARLY CLOSING DAY.

Ile would .like to suggest that it might be a good thing for churchgoing if the tradespeople of the town had their weekday half-holiday on Saturday afternoons instead of Thursday after- noons, and it would coincide with the works' half-holiday. He felt sure there would be a better attendance at church, as the tradesmen for the most part, under present arrangements. were unable to retire to rest till the early hours of Sunday morning, hence their indisposition to rise early. Ile thought also that if the men were paid on Friday evenings their wives could make their purchases for the week-end quite easily by noon on Saturday, and there would be less temptation for the men to spend their wages in the public-houses on Saturday after- noons.

div.head: DIVINE CHASTENING. God's Purpose in the Present NVar. BISHOP ELDRIDGE AT EMMANUEL.
div.p: DIVINE CHASTENING. God's Purpose in the Present NVar. BISHOP ELDRIDGE AT EMMANUEL.

Avery large congregation assembled on Sun- day evening at the Emmanuel Church, Bold- 'street, when a special service in connection with the " Come-to-Church " campaign was cat- ducted by the Rt. Rev. Dr. P. K. Eldridge (pre- siding bishop of the Reformed Episcopal Church) and the Rev. W. T. Jaye (incumbent). Preaching upon the text (Psalm cxviii. 1): "0 give thanks unto the Lord; for He is good: ,for His mercy endureth for ever," The Bishop pointed out that the Psalmist in- vited first all the nation at large; then the ofilcial representatives of the national religion; then, widening his invitation, the proselytes; and, lastly, his own personal friends. The invitation was one to which we, too, were called, both in our public and personal devotion. But it was not an exercise of common formality, coming formally before God as what we might call 3ur duty. It was praise, feelingly expressed, rush- ing ci om our hearts in a full tide of thanksgiv- ing. Then the Psalmist not only bade us to give thanks unto the Lord, but he added the reason—" because He is good and because His mercy endmeth for ever." "Those Twin Angels." . .

There were very many of these reasons. The general reason for praising God seemed to have two pat. The general reason was because He wa.: good and His mercy endured for ever. Good- ness and mercy—those twin angels which fol- lowed close behind and shadowed, on the right hand and on the left, every child of God! Good- ness was peculiarly a quality of God. He was not unwisely indulgent; on the other hand, His doings indicated a thoroughness of care whiA did away with any possibility of unkindness on MI part There was no desire of men that Be would tot recognise if that recognition would bring no pain. In the gift of .Nature God had shown Ills goodness—in the gift of Jesus lie huh revealed it.
Much Prayer, Little Praise.

Then there was His mercy. Mercy lay in God as its spring, as its source; and whu,t we could give of mercy was as a tiny stream by a full-flowing sea. Had we not many a fime re- ceived of this mercy? God had not failed—" His mercy endureth for ever." Every good gift called for thankigivlng, and every good gift of which we were unworthy called for more thanksgiving and every good gift for which we had not asked called for still more thanksgiving. Had we not called upon God in the time of trouble? Had we not only recently, as a nation, been on our knees beseeching God in our national pain? However much we might forget to speak to Him in time of peace, when God wanted to hear our voice, He had only to send us some trouble and we had fresh inspiration to pray. Were there not many occasions in our experience, in which we had been in perplexity and distress, when we cried as feebly as some little child and God heard? Oh, that praise might oftener follow prayer! We prayed so much; we praised so little.

div.head: God On Our Side.
div.p: God On Our Side.

Then the Psalmist gave another reason for our returning thanks—deliverance from danger: "The Lord is my strength and my song, and has become my salvation." The Psalmitt re; presented his position as one of peril, and we could apply these words to our own case. We had been forced into as great and terrible a war as the pages of history were ever likely to record. A great nation had been prepared with subtle designs to come against us, and we were in distress. Yet God was on our side, although we were not yet out of the wood: We should probably have to endure personal loss and grief. But had there been not past deliverances from danger for which we could thank God, and from. which we might anticipate help iu time of need?

div.head: ANNUAL RALLY.
div.p: THE ANNUAL RALLY.
Mayor on Adult School Principles.

The aims and ideals of the Adult School movement—which has . made rapid strides throughout the length and breadth of the coun- try, since its indeption a few years ay—formed the theme of speeches delivered in the Park Picture Palace, Warrington, on Sunday after- noon, when was held the annual rally of mem- bers of the local schools. The Mayor (Alder- ;llan Peter Peacock) presided, and was sup- ported on the platform by Messrs. David P. Boyd (Manchester) and William Grimshaw (Blackburn), and there was a fair attendance. WIDE AND COMPREHENSIVE MOVEMENT

The proceedings having opened with the sing- ing of a hymn, -His Worship said that since he last had the pleasure of presiding at one of their gatherings a lot of things had happened to throw gloom and sadness over the country, and Warrington had not been without its full share of that gloom and sadness. A lot of those who last year were assembled at a gathering similar to that were now doing their duty for their country at the front, serving gallantly with our gallant Army. When they contemplated the happen- sings of the day they stood aghast with wonder- ment,as to why the big natiOns of the world could not decide to settle their differences in a better way than an appeal to arms. (Hear, hear.) 'The spectacle of war-gripped Europe set them wondering why there could not exist a spirit of brotherhood amongst the different nations; why they could not exist in harmony? If a spirit similar to that existing within the Adult School movement existed between the peoples of different nationalities, the whole world would be the happier. (Hear, hear.) He said "within that movement" because it was a movement that knew no politics, no particular kind of religion and no differences of nationality but was wide and comprehensive. If the Adult Sehool principles could be made world-wide, he was sure -that the -world would be much .better:. it would be much better if it Were possible for its disputes to be settled at a kind of confer- ence—settled in a spirit of brotherhood. But, unfortunately, that was, so far, not possible. He hoped that the Adult Schools would con- tinue to prosper in the future, and that the men who were left behind inside, them, as well as many more men who were not yet members, but would, he trusted, shortly become such, would see to it that they carried on their useful work undiminished despite the very severe times the country was going through. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: GOOD TRAINING GROUND.
div.p: A GOOD TRAINING GROUND.

Mr. Grinishaw then briefly addressed the gath- ering. The Adult Schools of the country, he opined, constituted one of the best training grounds iewas possible for the men and women of •to-day to have. (Hear, hear.) He spoke from experience; for, largely, all that he was and all that he could do, was due to his train- ing in an Adult School. (Applause.) Within the movement even the humblest among them found glorious opportunities for doing some- thing. A PERSONAL TESTIMONY.

Mr. Boyd next spoke. The Adult Schools, he believed, had made a better man of him. They had given him a deeper sympathy for humanity; through them he had a greatei idea and ideal of God. and, because thereof, a greater love for his fellows. When he became associated with the movement he found that a lot of his old, narrow thoughts and ideas began to drop away, and new thoughts, new conceptions of life and its problems, came into their place. The dark- est cloud always preceded the dawn, and so it was in that movement. They were passing through times of crisis, and already they were beginning, to learn and to perceive, on the hori- zon, signs of the brightness that heralded the breaking day; they were beginning to realise, as Christian men and women, that these were days for closing up their, ranks and for consoli- dating their good work—times for subjecting themselves to the process of self-examination; times for finding out not only whether they believed, but why they believed!

div.head: %Faith As To The Future.
div.p: %Faith As To The Future.

They had sufficient faith in their movement— backed, he believed, by sufficient faith in them- selves—to believe that it was going to grow, and grow greatly until it became a big factor. In- cidentally the speaker said that one of the Adult Schools in Stockport had given fifteen out of thirty members to the service of King and country, and added that as the men were leaving the school's, up and down the country, to join the forces, their womenfolk were flocking into them, so that the loss of one branch of school work was the gain of the other. One of the most remarkable things about the Adult School movement was the variety of thought and men which it embraced; indeed, he ques- tioned whether there was in existence any other religious organisation that was composed of so many different kinds of •people, and yet had ,so little misunderstanding or ill-feeling among its members. (Hear, hear.) Within the Adult Schools, social standing was nothing, and poli- tics counted not at all; even differences of religious thought mattered nothing. Striving for High Ideals. _ _

One object anim-ated them, and that was to find some common ground for action; to strive together to find the best, and, having found it, live up to it. (Hear, hear.) One thing they realised, and that was that God could only triumph through human instrumentality; that He could only revolutionise the world, spiritu- ally, through the hearts and minds of ordinary men and women. God worked through the in- strumentality of men; through the personality of men and women, and before God could do His work they had to put themselves in an atti- tude for God to work by and through them. There must be a spirit of willingness and help- fulness in their hearts and minds. (Applause.) Between the speeches Miss Hewitt rendered in delightful fashion two suitable sacred solos, Mr. Trow accompanying on the pianoforte.

div.head: MR. GROSFEELD'S GIFT AND HINTS.
div.p: MR. GROSFEELD'S GIFT AND HINTS.

Re-organised along new and popular lines, the Warrington Junior Liberal Club and Associa- tion is looking forward to a fresh era of pros- perity and usefulness, and already new members are flocking to it in a manner and in numbers that must be distinctly encouraging to those who have been entrusted with the management of the organisation—an organisation which, in the past, has accomplished much good work in the cause of Liberalism in the town. That the Juniors have been of great service to the cause in the past is evidenced by the keen interest which the Seniors are taking in the re-organised club, many of the local leaders, from Mr. Cros- field downward, have hastened forward with promises of help and advice, which added to the strenuous efforts being put forth by the new officers to further enhance the popularity and attractiveness of the cosy headquarters in Horse- market-street, should absolutely ensure the future success of the organisation.

FURTHER POPULARISING THE CLUB. At the annual meeting of the club last week it was decided by a big majority to add a bar to the club for the sale of refreshments of all kinds, whilst at the adjourned annual meeting held in the Club roonis on Wednesday of this week, further steps to enhance the popularity of the club—already comfortably furnished and equipped with a delightful billiard room—were taken. New blood was infused into the man- agement.

Wednesday night's meeting,/whichas mainly called for the purposes of electing officers for the ensuing year, was presided over by Mr. Geo. Toulmin, who was supported by Mr. A. Andrews (acting secretary), and Mr. E., A. Sanders (Liberal agent), there being an excellent attend- ance of members.
ALDERMAN TINNION PROMISES HELP.
At the outset Alderman TINNms looked in, and, whilst regretting that a prior engagement prevented him staying for the meeting, prom- ised every assistance in his power.
MR. CROSFIELD OFFERS SUGGESTIONS.

Mr. 'shamus (Mr. Crosfield's private secre- tary), Nib° was also present during the early part of the proceedings, read a letter from the prospective Liberal candidate, which gave the members much cause for satisfaction. Seeing, he wrote, that that meeting had been called for the purpose of electing officers, &c., he felt, in view of the situation in which he was placed, that it would be rather a delicate matter for him to give advice one way or another, and for that reason he had concluded that it would be better for him not to attend that night, and, therefore, he had made other arrangements. He was sure that they would not construe his absence into meaning any lack of interest— (hear, hear)—for the fact was very far from that; indeed, he hoped ,that it was unnecessary for him to have to assure them that the very opposite was the case. (Hear, hear.) Far from feeling any lack of interest in the club, he took the keenest interest in it, and he would closely watch the fresh start which, with whole-hearted determination, the Juniors were making, with the object of ensuring that their club should be one of the most successful institutions in the town.

div.head: Useful Source of Revenue Waiting to be Tapped.
div.p: Useful Source of Revenue Waiting to be Tapped.

It seemed to him, Mr. Crosfield added, that there was scarcely a limit to the good use that such a club as theirs could make of the beauti- ful Memorial Hall in Bewsey-street.• Dances, whist drives, and other entertainments therein were bound 'to prove a most useful source of revenue to the Juniors, as also should their annual garden party. The caretaker of the Junior Club had informed him that more use would be made of the billiard table and conse- quently a better revenue derived if it were made possible for the members to play other games besides billiards on the table. He perfectly agreed, and he promised the caretaker there and then to provide a set of snooker balls. (Ap- plause.) A letter which he had received from the Chairman said: "You need have no fear that any advice you may offer to the Junior Liberals would give them the opinion that they are being put into leading strings, except, per- haps, the leading strings of Liberalism." Ile thanked them very much for that assurance, and could tell them that any suggestion that he might make would be made by way of sugges- tion only, and that he should not, in fife—least, think of doing anything in the way of dictation. For instance, it had been suggested to him that it would not be a bad plan to close the bar at 11.30 at night, and he passed the suggestion on to them for consideration. Further, he would suggest that the sale of drink should be limited to the bar. Also, he certainly thought it would be a good thing, if they could manage to supply simple, yet excellent luncheons, and, for that matter, suppers as well, and he hoped that in a moderate way that sort 'of catering for the requirements of mem- bers might prove.a further and useful source of income.

div.head: Membership Already On the Up-Grade. _ _
div.p: Membership Already On the Up-Grade. _ _

Ile had been delighted to learn that already the membership under the new regime reached the substantial total of 65, and he confidently hoped that it would not be very long before they succeeded in doubling that figure--(hear, hear)—and so make sure of a most successful future. It would give him great personal pleasure if Mr. Toulmin could see his way clear to accept the chairmanship of the club. . "Of course," added the letter, "it goes with- out saying that the club cannot make its fresh start without the backing of guarantors, but I take it for granted that we shall be able to arrange that matter, and then, given active, sound, common-sense management, I have not a shadow of doubt of your success in the future; indeed, T think that you ought to achieve not only greater success than in the past, but a humming success." (Applause.)

div.head: GOOD WISHES.
div.p: GOOD WISHES.

The ACTING SECRETARY then read a letter from Mr. P. O'Brien, in which that gentleman re- gretted that a previous engagement prevented him attending the meeting, expressed hie good wishes, and trusted that the club was on the eve of re-embarking on a long and successful voyage of usefulness to the Liberal cause. (Ap- plause.)

div.head: MR. E. LLOYD JONES RESIGNS.
div.p: MR. E. LLOYD JONES RESIGNS.
Mr. ANDREWS next read a letter of resignation from the late Chairman (Mr. E. Lloyd Jones), who enclosed a cheque for a guinea towards the funds.

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD RE-ELECTED PRESIDENT
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD RE-ELECTED PRESIDENT

The election of officers for the ensuing year. was then proceeded with. The. CRAIRMAN proposed the re-election of Mr. Crosfield as president, remarking that that gentleman had been president since the incep- tion of the club and association, and nobody in Warrington could fill the position better than he. had done. Mr. Crosfield was full' of enthu- siasm on their behalf, and, when that club was started in' its present quarters, he showed his interest for it in a practical way by furnishing their rooms for them. In other ways he had helped them; indeed, he had assisted the club on more than one occasion in a manner which would be a lasting credit to him, and which should fire them with a determination to do something worth the doing for the cause of Liberalism in the future. (Applause.) • Mr. STANIAY WALKEZ seconded, and' ttke pre- position was carried with applause.

SCHOOLKEEPERS "JOIN UP.''

The minutes of the Education Committee dealt with at the monthly meeting on Monday evening indicated that leave of absence has been granted to the following, schoolkeepers during their period of military service, and that their nominees are to be paid in each ease such sums as, with the total 'Army pay and separation allowances, if any, received from the Government, will make up an amount equal to their full wages for the time being, viz., Hamil- ton-street School, Mr. A. Amongst the name of wounded "South Lan- eashires" just published in the official lists, is that of Corporal S. W. Boast. It is interesting to note that the Corporal (who belongs to his regiment's cycle corps) is a son of Lieutenant and Quartermaster 8. T. Boast, who for thir- teen years served at Orford Barracks, obtaining his commission two years ago, and who, to- gether with his brother, Sergt. J. Boast (also formerly of Warrington), was recently men- tioned in dispatches by Sir John French.

div.head: DI SAPPEARI 16 CASUALS. Are 'Weary Willies" Enlisting
div.p: DI SAPPEARI 16 CASUALS. Are 'Weary Willies" Enlisting
or Working?

Some striking returns showing a falling off in the number of "casuals," due to the war, were laid before the Warrington Board of Guardians, at their fortnightly meeting on Wednesday, by the Workhouse Master (Mr. W. Loxham). The returns set forth that during 1913, 17,385 casuals (16,032 men, 1,280 women, and 86 chil- dren) were admitted to the casual wards, as against 13,298 (12,557 men, 683 women, and 58 children) in 1914, a decrease of 4,060, (3,465 men, 567 women, and 28 children). The reduction was most noticeable since the commencement of the war. From August Ist to December 31st, 1913, 6,608 male casuals Were admitted, as against 3,928 this year; a decrease of 2,680. In the same period there was a reduction of 276 in the num- ber of women admitted, and a further decrease of 26 in the number of children.

"Marry of the regular casuals," the Master added, " have either joined the colours them- selves, or taken the places of workmen who have. It is very seldom an able-bodied mart 'under 40 years of age applies for admission. Another pleasing feature is the greatly reduced number of children. It is very gratifying to know that for five months only eight children have passed through our wards."
